By examining $B^0_s \to K^+K^-$ decays, we determined the "effective" lifetime of these decays to be 1.38 $\pm$ 0.06 (stat) $\pm$ 0.12 (syst) ps. This measurement was derived from a sample of 87.1 $\pm$ 4.4 pb$^{-1}$ of data collected using the LHCb detector at an 8 GeV center-of-mass energy. This measure of the lifetime allows for a better understanding of $B^0_s \to K^+K^-$ decay rates and rare processes mediated by electroweak interactions, specifically those involving closed loops of top quarks and $\gamma$ or $Z$ bosons. The precision of this measurement was found to be superior to existing estimates, which ranged from 1.5 to 2.0 ps. The resulting data were also used to determine the ratio of $B^0_s \to K^+K^-$ to $B^0 \to K^+\pi^0$ decay rates, yielding a value of $32.8 \pm 3.0$; this measurement was in line with theoretical predictions based on factorization approaches and asymptotic scaling in QCD. The precision of this measurement was found to be superior to existing estimates, which ranged from 20 to 30. The LHCb detector at the CERN particle accelerator provided the data used for these calculations. The upgrade of the LHCb detector, scheduled for installation in 2022, is expected to collect 50 times more data, enabling more precise calculations of decay rates and rare processes. The authors initially establish the existence and uniqueness of a solution to this problem, before transitioning to the examination of a suitable numerical scheme. They then analyze the asymptotic behavior of this discrete system, comparing it to the original continuous system. The purpose of this research is to provide insights into the properties of a specific numerical scheme, with potential applications to complex, real-world problems. The authors also discuss the results of this research, with particular reference to its connection to a previous study on a different numerical scheme. The asymptotic analysis of this discrete system also yields useful and readily interpretable metrics, with potential value to scholars and experts in the field. The findings of this research are formally presented in the form of theorems, with supporting evidence provided in the form of numerical examples and additional graphical analysis. The results presented in this research paper are relevant to a broader category of stochastic and deterministic systems, with potential connections to the study of complex systems at multiple scales. The purpose of this research is purely theoretical, with the aim of advancing the understanding of a specific numerical scheme, rather than addressing any of the many real-world problems that this scheme or similar schemes could potentially solve. An analysis of the clear surface of the Pierre Auger Observatory has led to the detection of extremely large cosmic-ray fluctuations on scales exceeding 6.4 million square meters, observed above 4 EeV, despite the lack of evidence for correlated signals in extensive air showers. A new metric is introduced to quantify these fluctuations, which are found to increase significantly with the size of the observed area, deviating from expected patterns of cosmic-ray distribution. Additionally, correlations between these fluctuations and the arrival directions of nearby cosmic rays are being investigated to better understand the origins of this phenomenon. Two possible explanations are proposed: either these fluctuations result from the interference of nearby, anisotropically distributed cosmic rays, possibly linked to massive cosmic structures, or they indicate the presence of highly variable sources of cosmic rays, likely situated within 12 million light-years. Further research is necessary to distinguish between these scenarios and uncover the underlying causes of these phenomena. A new, more sensitive detector being constructed in the Argentinian Pampa Amarilla site is expected to provide additional insights into these phenomena with its capacity to detect connected air showers and extensive observation of the clear surface of the detector.

This paper proves that any Zinbiel algebra, defined by the identity $xy(yz) = (xy)(yz)$ for all elements $x, y, z$, will necessarily satisfy the identity $xy(zw) = (zw)(xy)$ for all elements $x, y, z, w$. Consequently, it is demonstrated that the Zinbiel identity alone is equivalent to the Malcev identity, which is $[x,y][z,t] = [z,t][x,y]$, allowing us to classify these algebras using the established methods for Malcev algebras. Furthermore, it is shown that the Zinbien basis can be converted into the Malcev basis via a series of straightforward transformations, thereby establishing a connection between these two algebraic structures. Notably, this connection reveals that the variety of Zinbiel algebras over an arbitrary field is nilpotent of class two, finite-dimensional, and solvable, among other properties inherited from the corresponding properties of Malcev algebras. Lastly, this research also examines the specific case of Zinbiel algebras defined over the real numbers, uncovering that the only possible dimensions for its varieties are the powers of two.

This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and certain relationships between data entries. Our goal is to identify consistent data subsets that represent possible truth values for each data entry. We have developed a framework that combines techniques for handling inconsistent data and constraint satisfaction problems, incorporating methods for dealing with missing values and data relationships. Our framework facilitates efficient and scalable resolution of data discrepancies and can be applied to solve real-world problems. Moreover, our approach accommodates different discrepancy severity measures and data quality criteria, enabling us to prioritize the most critical errors and data entries. We have tested our framework on artificial and real-world datasets and compared it favorably to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our framework, along with experimental results and example use cases, is made available to the public.

Time series with counts as values often fluctuate significantly due to changes in time, making dynamic models with shifting parameters particularly relevant. In this research, we develop a novel approach, the Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregressive model of order one (TPAR(1)), to handle such count-based time series with changing parameters. Uniquely, the TPAR(1) model employs a non-degenerate version of the specification, with time-varying coefficients allowing for the exploration of seasonally changing patterns and temporally localized effects, without restricting periodic patterns. We establish theoretical fundamentals for the model, including moment conditions and asymptotic properties of estimation procedures. To evaluate the performance of the TPAR(1) model, we conduct simulations, revealing its advantages over fixed-parameter alternatives. Additionally, the efficacy of TPAR(1) is demonstrated through an empirical application and comparison with existing methods using three real-world datasets. The results show that the TPAR(1) model delivers superior fit and accurate predictions, with the benefit of incorporating interpretable time-varying coefficient estimates. The R package, tvpar, is also developed to facilitate the implementation of the TPAR(1) model and related models. The development of the TPAR(1) model introduces a novel approach to modeling temporal changes in time series with counts as values, and the associated package and R functions provide researchers with a useful tool for counting time series data. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel framework that generates
robust and 3D rotation-invariant object representations, which we apply to
automated object manipulation tasks.  Our NDF architecture combines the
advantages of learning-based and regression-based methods for representing 3D
objects and incorporates a novel orientation-aware loss function to achieve
SE(3) invariance.  We utilize our NDF descriptor in a sorting-and-picking task
for object arrangement and demonstrate that our NDF outperforms competing
descriptors with 3D rotation-invariance properties, as proven by our
experiments.  Our results show that NDF yields a 27.4% higher success rate and
a 3.6-fold decrease in failure cases when compared to the current state-of-the-
art.  Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/vishalraviteja/ndf.

These values supplement earlier predictions made using a one-loop expansion. Notably, our findings indicate that the edge singularity's position is independent of whether the system exhibits a first- or second-order phase transition. In statistics and machine learning, a fundamental tool is the sum of square-free minimization, crucial for estimating the performance of various algorithms. This target function can be efficiently computed using the TAP method, yielding an approximation of the free energy in the Gibbs measure. Our research verifies that the TAP-free energy function has a local concave structure when applied to random instance ensembles from a broad generation process. This finding is particularly significant because it underpins the validity of the AMP (Algebraic Message Passing) algorithm and facilitates a alternative proof of the local concavity of the TAP free energy in random Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models. Additionally, we establish the occurrence of a phase transition in random linear systems employing the Sudakov-Fernique-AMP approach, which also yields an alternative to the standard proof of the Guerra-Talagrand-Mémoli theorem. This result showcases the versatility of the AMP framework in modeling phase transitions in random system contexts. Lastly, our research provides an alternative to the standard proof of the BLP theorem, which is a key result in the theory of random regular graphs. This finding demonstrates the wide applicability of the AMP framework in modeling random graph instances. Lastly, we examine the variance of the TAP-free energy estimate, which is an unexplored aspect of the theory. This research was originally published in ScienceDirect.

While using photometry from stars to assess the atmosphere may seem like a straightforward concept, taking into consideration the numerous factors that affect the transmission of light through the atmosphere has proven to be a complex task. The accuracy of previous studies that used photometry to measure atmospheric properties, particularly aerosol levels, has been questioned due to limited knowledge of atmospheric conditions in the relevant regions. A study was conducted to re-analyze previous observations of the atmosphere in the Sahel region using photometry from the OMI satellite, with a focus on validating previous findings. Although previous research had suggested low aerosol levels in the region, the re-analysis revealed a more aerosol-affected area, with a mean optical depth of 0.23 in the northwestern part of the Sahel during its dry season. A notable correlation was also observed between the optical depth and vegetation coverage in the area. A model was then developed to estimate the optical depth based on vegetation coverage, which could potentially be used as a proxy for other atmospheric properties affected by vegetation and aerosols. A key finding of this study is that it is essential to account for the varying levels of vegetation coverage and its impact on atmospheric properties when conducting research in regions with diverse land use. This knowledge is particularly relevant for studies of the Amazon rainforest, the Congo basin, and other similar regions with high levels of vegetation coverage and significant impacts from land use. It is also crucial to consider the effects of vegetation and land use on atmospheric properties when conducting research in these areas, which could provide new insights and help mitigate the effects of land use on the atmosphere, particularly in relation to cloud and aerosol formations. It is also worth noting that the relationship between vegetation coverage and optical depth could vary across different regions, and more research is needed to validate this finding across other areas. This study used data from the OMI satellite and the MODIS terra instrument, with a focus on the Sahel region during the dry season, from 2005 to 2019. The re-analysis of previous observations uncovered a seasonal pattern of aerosol levels in the Sahel region during the dry season, with higher levels of aerosols in the northern part of the region. This pattern may be related to the burning of vegetation in the region during this period. This finding has important implications for modeling the atmosphere in the Sahel region during the dry season, with suggestions to incorporate vegetation burning into models of aerosol levels in this area. Recently, a significant surge in pose estimation with full degrees of freedom (DoF) has been seen, primarily driven by advancing robotics and autonomous navigation requirements. Overcoming fundamental challenges like self-occlusion and correspondence ambiguity is crucial for this development. To tackle these difficulties, this work introduces the DeepHMap++ framework, which integrates two critical tasks: projection grouping and correspondence learning. Projection grouping is a pre-processing step to reduce projection ambiguity by identifying distinct projective regions, each corresponding to a distinct pose. On the other hand, correspondence learning directly aims to find correspondences between images and 3D models, leveraging the rich information provided by projection grouping. We introduce a combined loss function that combines the consistency loss of correspondences derived from projection grouping and 3D-2D matching, leading to a 60 times speedup in our experiments. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conduct a series of experiments on the DTU and BenAbdelfadil datasets, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is versatile and the source code is available at: \url{https://github.com/lingyu1993/DeepHMap}.

Traditional molecular dynamics methods are compromised by their requirement for precise configurations, hampering their use in complex systems, particularly in biology and chemistry. This limitation motivates the development of more robust numerical methods for time-stepping, with the aim of making configurational sampling more efficient. In the context of Langevin dynamics, with its built-in temperature control, we explore two key objectives for time-stepping algorithms: ensuring that generated configurations are both sufficiently precise and easily accepted in subsequent Metropolis tests. To this end, we introduce two key metrics: the precision of configurational sampling, reflected in the distribution of pairwise interactions between atoms, and the Metropolis acceptance rate, a indicator of the suitability of generated configurations. Through extensive simulations of Lennard-Jones clusters, polypeptide chains, and a fullerene molecule, we establish that HPM methods generally excel in both measures. In particular, we find that fourth-order HPM exhibits a notable advantage over its third-order counterpart. Moreover, our analysis uncovers the relationship between the precision of configurational sampling and the strength of interactions within the system, demonstrating that the distribution of pairwise interactions converges to a known distribution as the system size increases. In the process, we rectify an earlier error regarding this distribution and propose a simple yet effective way to determine an optimal time-step size for simulations. Lastly, we propose a scheme for dynamically adjusting the time-step size in response to changing system size or the strength of atomic interactions, with accompanying computational cost. In the course of our investigation, we discovered that the standard metric for evaluating time-stepping algorithms, total energy error, is an inadequate measure, as it prioritizes precision over the efficiency of configurational sampling, leading to questionable recommendations. In contrast, our results suggest a time-step size of $h=\sqrt[3]{\Delta t^3+N^{-1}}$ yields both precise and acceptable configurations, with total energy error and Metropolis acceptance rate both converging to specific values as the system size increases. In the context of a specific simulation, we demonstrate that this time-step size enables the correct folding of a polypeptide chain at a given temperature, in contrast to a fixed time-step size that results in incorrect folding. In the process, we provide a clear and concise derivation of the relationship between the distribution of pairwise interactions and the precision of configurational sampling, along with a graphical representation of this relationship. Our research introduces a new method for identifying the most distinctive nodes within complex multilayer networks by analyzing the eigenvectors of a combined, hypergraph-based transition matrix. Unlike traditional approaches that prioritize central nodes, our method highlights nodes that exhibit significant differences in their corresponding layers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by incorporating a modified centrality measure, called eigenvector prominence, which accounts for the multilayer structure and provides a significance ranking for each node across the network. Our findings show that this approach outperforms single-layer eigenvector centrality in various network analysis tasks, including node classification, graph reconstruction, and the detection of influential spreaders. To facilitate the application of our method to real-world multilayer networks, we provide a user-friendly Python implementation of the algorithm along with an example dataset consisting of multilayer social networks. Our results are also compared to those obtained using the multilayer node salience measure, which is based on the same hypergraph framework but uses a different eigenvector weighting scheme. Our research and associated code are available online at https://github.com/EVVector.

This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being pressed into contact with it, a phenomenon known as seal or laminar entry. Unraveling this process, which occurs at water speeds ranging from 0.2 to 10 meters per second, reveals its underlying causes. Researchers have long believed that spheres create a stable, long-lasting seal through centrifugal force. However, our findings show that this theory is only partially true and that the behavior of spheres in this scenario is actually determined by their size in relation to the water flow, not their weight. They also discover that spheres with diameters greater than three times the height of the water flow form a permanent seal, while those with smaller diameters may form a temporary or no seal at all. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the shape of the water flow around the sphere remains the same regardless of its size, and that the pressure exerted on the sphere increases in a particular way with the speed of the water flowing over it. This research also examines how the shape of the sphere and the characteristics of the water flowing over it affect this interaction, but finds that only the size of the sphere plays a significant role in this process. This study's findings are presented in a set of mathematical equations that can be used to predict the behavior of spheres interacting with running water. This research was conducted to better understand how water flows over objects, particularly those with curved surfaces, and could have applications in fields such as hydroelectric power generation, naval design, and the study of water flowing over plants and other natural objects. This knowledge could also be used to improve the accuracy of mathematical models used to simulate the movement of water and other fluids over complex surfaces. This study focuses specifically on the interaction between water and spheres, but the principles it reveals could be applied to the study of water flowing over other curved surfaces. A novel phenomenon called the Rabi cycle can occur when an external field resonates a quantum system, causing energy and probability to oscillate between two states. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper structure, specifically examining a herringbone lattice with glide symmetry. This lattice exhibits both semi-metallic and insulating behavior, depending on the adjustment of its parameters. Notably, we find that its geometry gives rise to Dirac points that can be modified in response to external pressure applied along certain high-symmetry paths, and we identify three distinct types of adjustable Dirac points within this system. Moreover, we find that adjusting the lattice's parameters can shift these points, merge them into a single loop, or split them into multiple discrete points. Furthermore, we examine how these Dirac points behave under strain and potential misalignment of the lattice, and demonstrate that its unique properties can be realized in an experimental setting using a herringbone lattice of black phosphorus or silicene layers stacked at a 30-degree angle. Our findings suggest that this system's versatile Dirac points, combined with its 2D topology and adjustable parameters, make it an appealing subject for in-depth investigation.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states possess a specific trait: they only emit a photon when a signal beam is detected, and the resulting photon is highly entangled with the initial coherent state. These states could be useful for a variety of quantum applications, including quantum simulation, metrology, and state storage. However, generating them is challenging due to the lack of a controlled single-photon emission source. In this work, we demonstrate that it's possible to create these states without a single-photon emitter, leveraging quantum-optical catalysis in a cavity filled with nonlinear media. We develop a practical approach to produce these states in systems based on parametric amplifiers and demonstrate the feasibility of implementing them using current technology, including linear optical elements and nonlinear devices like optical parametric amplifiers. We also explore the relationship between the state preparation method and the detection of these states, highlighting the potential for directly observing single-photon facilitated coherent states through homodyne detection. Furthermore, we analyze the effectiveness of this approach in generating states that could be useful for quantum simulation and investigate the connection to other quantum states and phenomena.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the fundamental role of bivectors becomes apparent under the transformation of electromagnetic tensors and the Weyl curvature tensor. This paper delves into the specifics of these transformations, starting with the well-established conversion from electromagnetic tensors to bivectors, and the less well-known process of converting the Weyl tensor's electric part from its complex self-dual form to a real form utilizing bivectors. The latter process is particularly important as it provides a direct link between the Weyl tensor's electric and magnetic components, which are often referred to as the Petrov's classification coefficients. The proposed approach also facilitates the computation of these coefficients without resorting to the use of complex conformal curvature tensors. The relationship between the Weyl tensor's components can be further analyzed to define the conditions for alignment with respect to Killing tensors of the second kind, which are crucial for understanding the physical implications of some cosmological models. The discussion on the Newman-Penrose formalism concludes with the conversion of the Weyl tensor's complex self-dual form to a real form using bivectors, which allows for the direct comparison of the Einstein tensor with respect to the Killing tensor of the second kind. The paper also explores the implications of the Weyl tensor's decay in the context of the cosmological principle, which leads to the recovery of the Friedmann-Lema\^itre equations, along with a relevant numerical example. Traditional symbolic techniques used in program analysis, such as abstract interpretation, can produce precise results by leveraging learning-based methods, although their initial cost may be high. We propose a new approach, the Polymers technique, which utilizes a specific combination of learning and solving components to determine the polymers (a concept analogous to monomers in program analysis) associated with a statement in a program. Given that the number of polymers is typically limited, we employ an integer optimization problem to determine this count, and use a linear regression-based approach, clover, to create a data structure that can efficiently capture complex relationships among variables. Once the polymers are established, we can incorporate them into the abstract semantical environment to update the state of the program, facilitating further analysis. We have implemented this technique in the Soot Java framework and tested it on benchmark programs, demonstrating a significant reduction in the time and memory required for its escape analysis. Furthermore, we have conducted an in-depth financial cost/benefit analysis of this approach on real-world applications, demonstrating that the Polymers technique can yield desirable outcomes when the initial setup cost is low relative to the savings achieved. The source code for this technique is available online at github.com/awpl/Polymers.

Early detection of esophageal neoplasms is critical, and automating their detection using CT image analysis can be quite useful.
This research focuses on developing a reliable and efficient method for categorizing normal, benign, and malignant esophageal neoplasms from low-dose CT scans.
A novel network called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, designed specifically for this task, incorporates both spatial and channel attention mechanisms to concentrate on high-importance features, and it utilizes dilated convolutional layers to handle small CT scan resolutions.
To evaluate the proposed network, a custom esophageal neoplasm segmentation task was created, and it showed superior performance compared to conventional methods. 
This is particularly notable as it achieved a significant 6.1% improvement in the AUC-ROC metric for distinguishing malignant from benign neoplasms.
This work demonstrates the potential of the Dilated Dense Attention Unet to excel in related tasks, such as lesion detection and density estimation, and it provides a dataset that other researchers can utilize for further development. 
The associated code and dataset are available online at \url{https://github.com/ghr95/DenseUnet_Esoph}. 
This network has been successfully applied in a clinical setting, and it can be employed as a starting point for developing models for related but distinct esophageal neoplasm analysis problems. 
For instance, a model has been developed to predict the type of esophageal neoplasm based on segmentation results, and it demonstrated excellent performance, and another one has been developed to estimate the density of neoplasms, and it showed a low error rate. 
This work highlights the value of using low-dose CT scans, which result in a 90% reduction in radiation exposure, without any decrease in accuracy. 
This reduction in radiation also results in a 30% decrease in analysis time.

Code-mixed languages, which combine elements from two different languages, are a common mode of communication in multilingual societies, particularly among community members who possess basic knowledge of multiple languages. This code-mixed practice serves various purposes, including enhancing clarity and simplifying complex linguistic expressions, and it allows for easier online content consumption and creation. Notably, it presents an significant challenge for NLP systems, which are typically trained on monolingual data. A code-mixed trained model, on the other hand, can be highly beneficial as it can be fine-tuned for multiple languages with minimal effort. We explore the difficulties NLP systems face when dealing with code-mixed data and the opportunities it presents, and we discuss several important aspects such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, and dialogue systems. With enough code-mixed data, it is possible to develop highly adaptable multilingual models that can be easily trained for a wide range of tasks and applications. We highlight the importance of code-mixed NLP in areas like customer service and internet content moderation, and we outline potential research and practical challenges along with feasible solutions, including the utilization of pre-trained multilingual models, pseudo-labeling, and the creation of large code-mixed datasets. Ultimately, this survey aims to stimulate innovative ideas and encourage research in code-mixed NLP. We also include an appendix that contains a code-mixed dataset creation guidelines for various tasks and applications.

The evaluation of automatic image descriptions relies on human-provided references, which rarely account for diverse descriptions. Consequently, a gap exists in the data, making it necessary to create additional datasets that incorporate a variety of descriptions. In this work, we leverage employee descriptions from an e-commerce platform for images, which we believe to be a suitable source of such diverse descriptions. We examine the utility of these employee descriptions in assessing the quality of automatic image descriptions generators. To this end, we developed a novel evaluation metric that compares the similarity between human references and employee descriptions. We also explored a simpler approach based on description frequency. Both metrics demonstrated a meaningful connection to human evaluation scores. Notably, the novel metric exhibited a superior fit to the data and more accurately captured the performance of state-of-the-art generators. Our research is significant because it offers a practical solution to the description diversity problem and provides generators with valuable information to improve their performance. Moreover, our results are intriguing because they reveal that employee descriptions that are less accurate are actually more diverse, and that there is a gap in this diversity when comparisons are made with other images. This research is relevant to multiple fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and e-commerce. Moreover, the employee descriptions used in this study are distinct from traditional reference descriptors. This distinction arises from the fact that these descriptions were created for a different purpose, with a focus on enticing customers to purchase images rather than providing a detailed, accurate description. This difference is critical because it makes these descriptions diverse, as they include a variety of styles and terms. This diversity is absent from traditional reference descriptors, which are often precise but varied only in terms of formatting. This work provides a novel approach to assessing the quality of generators, as well as a solution to the diversity problem. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have synthesized Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles with remarkable optical and electrical characteristics. Nevertheless, the absence of a standard reference for the Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structure complicates material analysis and nanoparticle synthesis. This study aims to determine the fundamental crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ using ab initio simulations and Monte Carlo methods. Initially, the authors used DFT and GLSA simulations to examine different Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs before carrying out experimental reflection and X-ray absorption measurements to match their results with the data. Consequently, they focused on the most plausible $\gamma$-phase structure on which they performed extensive Monte Carlo simulations to determine the lattice parameter, $c$, as well as the Ta and O site occupation distributions. Furthermore, they compared their theoretical findings with experimental reflection and X-ray absorption spectra in order to gain a deeper understanding of how Ta$_2$O$_5$ is structured at both the local and global levels. The results of this study are expected to facilitate effortless comparison of their simulation data with experimental outcomes, in addition to guiding future synthesis and characterization efforts for Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles. The $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state crystal structure is now publicly available for scientific reference.

This research investigates the significance of a social hierarchy, referred to as the Big Geographic Sort, in spreading misinformation on Reddit. The Big Geographic Sort encompasses a pattern of residential segregation observed across major American cities, where residents of urban areas tend to interact more with people living in urban settings compared to those living in suburban or rural areas. This project seeks to explore the implications of the Big Geographic Sort on the propagation of misinformation by examining the relationship between a user's city of residence and their likelihood of sharing false information. The study utilizes a large dataset of alleged misinformation from the claimedit.io platform and combines it with user location data from the Reddit platform. The results reveal that users residing in urban areas are more prone to sharing false information, and this propensity is particularly evident in larger cities. Furthermore, an analysis of commenting patterns reveals that the Big Geographic Sort contributes to the fragmentation of online communities, which in turn facilitates the dissemination of misinformation. The study's findings have broader implications for the understanding of the Big Geographic Sort and its connection to social trust and the efficacy of truth-seeking mechanisms in urban settings. The role of the Big Geographic Sort in promoting the credibility of online information and the resilience of megacities to misinformation and other dangers is also discussed. The study's methods and data are available for public use. The findings presented in this research paper appear to be specific to the Reddit user base, and future research is needed to verify these findings in other online platforms and megacity contexts. The study's conclusions are based on the observation that the Big Geographic Sort accelerates the propagation of misinformation on Reddit, but the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon require further investigation. The study also highlights the potential of Reddit user location data and claims fact-checking initiatives as tools for studying the Big Geographic Sort and its effects. The research paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for future research, including the examination of the Big Geographic Sort's relationship to online information quality, social trust, and megacity resilience, as well as the development of mathematical models that incorporate the Big Geographic Sort and online information dynamics. Humans follow spoken instructions effortlessly, yet the underlying process is complex.  As robots integrate into daily life, understanding how they process audio instructions is crucial.  Research on speech processing for robots typically employs synthesized audio, but using real speech from human instructors provides more authentic instruction.  This study observes human instructors guiding a robot through various manipulation tasks and examines how they structure their speech.  Twenty-four instructors guided a robot through three different tasks, with two variants of each task.  The results show that humans use a consistent pattern of introducing tasks, referencing the robot's actions, and providing feedback.  A notable finding is that instructors often deviate from a standard pattern, possibly due to the natural flow of conversation.  The research highlights opportunities to improve speech instruction for robots by considering natural language protocols.  Such protocols could enhance the effectiveness of speech instructions in real-world settings by promoting clear, consistent audio that robots can easily interpret.  This study's findings and natural language protocol suggestions can be applied across various domains where robots receive spoken instructions.  The data is available for public use.  This work is part of the larger research project called Activity Understanding for Collaborative Systems.  The project aims to develop a unified framework for a robot to anticipate and understand human activities during collaborative tasks.  The framework consists of three interconnected components: activity prediction, action recognition, and speech understanding.  The data and code are available at \url{https://github.com/ActivityUnderstanding}.  The framework and an associated protocol are discussed in detail in the project's main paper [1]. Conversational systems relying on AI have gained significant traction, and their popularity continues to grow. While these systems have achieved a high level of success, their underlying technology lacks a well-defined framework, and their components are not well-articulated. This lack of structure and clear components makes it challenging to develop a testing framework for these systems. To address this difficulty, we introduce a novel MTSES (Multi-Threaded Semantic Error Specification and Validation for Conversational Systems with Memory) methodology that focuses on conversational systems with memory. This approach enables the validation of specified behaviors and the discovery of system errors by simulating system-conversational interactions. Our case study involving a bot that utilizes memory to conduct natural language inquiries demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach. The data from this example, along with previous research, show that MTSES leads to a significant reduction in the discovery of new system errors compared to traditional approaches. Our framework, consisting of the MTSES methodology and a corresponding toolchain, is available open-source. This toolchain includes a simulator, a specification language, and the MTSES validator, and it can be accessed at https://mtses.github.io/. This framework supports the validation of conversational systems and provides a command line interface for the simulator. Our data on system error discoveries, which are relevant to the community, are also available open-source at https://mtses.github.io/mtses-at-icse-2021-data.zip. Cross-domain recommendation has gained significant attention for addressing the growing issue of data scarcity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR models have been developed to cater to various real-world scenarios, including multi-sparse-domain scenarios, multi-target CDR, and multi-domain collaborative filtering. However, research on multi-sparse-domain CDR remains limited due to the difficulty of training models when there are few data points in each of the sparse domains. Existing models, such as GCR and CKE, which handle multi-target and multi-domain scenarios, may not be effective in multi-sparse-domain settings because they fail to fully utilize cross-domain information when data is scarce in each of the sparse domains. Therefore, we present a new model called MSCDR that combines the strengths of attribute-aware and graph-based methods to fully leverage cross-domain information. MSCDR utilizes attribute preferences to capture cross-domain information and builds a graph to incorporate the influence of each data point on the model parameters. Conic programs are highly effective for a broad spectrum of optimization tasks but can fall short if the underlying mathematics isn't well understood. While solver software efficiently handles the practical aspects, it can complicate the representation of certain key elements, particularly conic expressions arising from natural phenomena. These fundamental expressions, such as rotated second-order cone and primal-dual interior-point, can be challenging to formulate directly within standard conic programming frameworks. This issue is particularly pronounced in data science applications, where high-dimensional data often employs non-linear relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce the Hypatia conic formulation toolkit, specifically designed to provide a more intuitive and descriptive framework for formulating conic models. This tool allows researchers to focus on the underlying mathematical structure of their problems, unencumbered by the constraints of standard conic formulations. As a proof of concept, we apply Hypatia to resolve several key conic expressions, demonstrating a more direct and intuitive path to formulating models. This approach is further illustrated with an analysis of word frequencies in Jane Austen's novels, a classic example of multi-dimensional data that incorporates non-linear relationships. This work is made available through the Hypatia.jl Julia package, which can be easily installed using the Julia REPL by running `Pkg.add("Hypatia")`. This package is also compatible with popular solver software, including JuMP, MOI, and CPLEX. The escalating number of MRI scans necessitates automated quality assessment to guarantee data reliability for critical medical applications such as neurological research and clinical diagnostics. This paper presents a novel approach to MRI data assessment, focusing on the analysis of data collected under different research protocols. Unlike conventional approaches that categorize data based on individual protocol features, our method develops a framework to combine protocol characteristics, enabling the prediction of image data features across a range of protocols. We evaluate this framework on real MRI data and demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing inherent similarities and differences between protocols, as well as in accurately classifying new, unseen data. This work is particularly relevant to closed research settings where data is collected under various, often inflexible protocols. Though real-world MRI acquisition protocols preclude complete control over scanning conditions, future work aims to expand this framework to accommodate more variable acquisition settings, common in open studies. This paper is the first in a series of three, each addressing a separate aspect of MRI data analysis: quality assessment, segmentation, and group comparison. The code for this work is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepHealthGroup/MRIQA. The results are also available on the CEREBRAT platform at https://cerebrat.org/.

It is demonstrated that charging electric cars from a local network can either increase or decrease the duration of stable operation, with this outcome being contingent upon various factors including grid configuration, electric car behavior, and charging patterns. A novel multi-agent optimization approach is presented to examine how privately owned electric cars influence the duration of stable operation when they are allowed to act autonomously. This method facilitates the examination of different scenarios and provides valuable insights into how privately owned electric cars can enhance the duration of stable operation, with a particular focus on distributing electric car charging across different time periods. This occurs because the relationship between peak load and duration of stable operation is nonlinear, with a particular pattern of load demand being necessary for the duration of stable operation to be maximized. In scenarios involving multiple agents working together towards a common goal, incentives can motivate cooperation by rewarding beneficial interactions. Our research focuses on a meeting model where agents collaborate to achieve a shared objective, and cooperation is encouraged through a drive-based incentive scheme. Unlike traditional approaches that solely punish malicious behavior, this framework incentivizes healthy interactions by fostering a desire to engage in cooperative activities. Our results show that by incorporating a specific type of incentive, known as the "driving" incentive, which encourages agents to prioritize other cars over obstacles, collaboration in the meeting scenario becomes significantly more effective. Furthermore, we find that a combination of drive and freeze incentives yields the best results, leading to a significant improvement in task completion time. Our findings on the drive-based incentive's effectiveness are particularly notable, as they contribute a novel insight to the study of distributed coordination systems. Our code is available online at github.com/GroupMindLab/MAM-RM. Moreover, we provide a solution to the issue of meeting termination, which is a common problem in similar scenarios, by introducing a "termination time" that limits the meeting duration. Our data is also publicly available on github.com/GroupMindLab/MAM-RM. Our research on the meeting scenario and its variants has yielded several interesting observations, which are presented in the supplementary materials. Our approach to implementing the incentive scheme and coordinating interactions relies on a simple Q-learning-based agent design and a distributed coordination algorithm called "F-DES", which enables efficient and cooperative behavior in the meeting scenario. This research extends the fundamental theorem initially established by Wajnrych to the exponential Coxeter systems of type B, providing a characterization of exchangeable transformations that fix the length of the 120-degree angle. Furthermore, it identifies the solvable case as a subset of the larger class of reversible systems and determines the precise structure of these systems. However, the extent to which this approach is feasible has not been previously examined. This study introduces a novel approach to apply the lensing effect to SNe data, focusing on the Pantheon SNIa dataset and a simplified lensing model. Cosmological parameters are estimated using this model and the results show that the uncertainty in the lensing effect of the void network around SNe does not exceed the current limits of error, allowing for a combination of SNe data with lensing, but indicating that this approach does not offer a independent means of estimating the Hubble constant. Nevertheless, this method and future observations will allow for the combination of SNe data with lensing effects in the void network around galaxies as foreground lenses, providing a new approach to investigate the fundamental properties of gravity and the cosmological scale. Nonlinear add-drop filters, an essential component in wavelength routers and certain types of processors, can be implemented using T-shaped resonators in photonic silicon-on-insulator material. Research has focused on a specific type of T resonators, where the bar and the T-shaped arm form a 90-degree angle, especially to reduce mode-field cross-talk. In this work, an analytical and numerical investigation of T resonators with any angle is conducted, and the results show that a 60-degree T resonator provides the optimal cross-talk reduction and offers more flexible design options. Moreover, this type of 60-degree T resonator allows for the creation of a ring resonator with a smaller size, which can accommodate more channels in a 2D array architecture. An example of a 5-channel 60-degree T resonator array is presented, and the results are verified using a silicon-on-insulator material at telecommunication frequencies. This type of T resonator can also be used to create a beam splitter or a nonlinear delay line. The findings of this research can be applied to other materials with a high Kerr nonlinearity, such as chalcogenide and germanium, but are particularly beneficial for silicon-on-insulator material due to its high Kerr nonlinearity and ease of fabrication. In a design for a 60-degree T resonator on a SOI substrate, a bar length of 5 micrometers and a bar and T-arm width of 0.5 micrometers were found to provide the optimal results. This type of T resonator can be integrated with a microresonator array or a photonic wire to create a reconfigurable and nonlinear photonic chip. In this design, the T resonator and the microresonator form a loop that contains a beta bar and a beta T, which can be calculated as follows: beta bar = (pi * r_res) / (2 * L_bar * d), beta T = (pi * r_res) / (2 * L_T * d), where r_res is the radius of the microresonator, L_bar and L_T are the lengths of the bar and the T-arm, and d is the thickness of the SOI substrate. In this example, beta bar = 3.14 * 1.5 / (2 * 5 * 220) = 0.0159, beta T = 3.14 * 1.5 / (2 * 4 * 220) = 0.0175

For our paper titled "Assessing Context for Deep Object Recognizers", we introduce a straightforward method to investigate the impact of surrounding elements on the accuracy of object detection models. By creating a library of overlay images, we can selectively add background objects to target classes within a pre-existing detection dataset. This approach allows us to identify areas of the image where context has the greatest impact on the task and to compare the effectiveness of different object detection models in utilizing this information. Our assessment of a leading detection model on the KITTI dataset reveals that its performance is largely insulated from the influence of surrounding objects except in specific cases, such as when the target is very small or in high-density traffic scenes. Moreover, we observe a subtle ability of the model to learn from the context, albeit without explicit training, which is further confirmed by a simple learning context-aware model that incorporates multi-resolution image processing. This model's performance surpasses the basic baseline by a 10% absolute improvement in average AP. Our research highlights the limited utilization of context in current object detection models and suggests avenues for improving their performance in real-world scenarios. Our code and overlay library are available online at the address given in the references.

Given a closed, symplectic $n$-manifold $(M,\omega)$ and a smooth, real $(n-2)$-manifold $P$, there exists a natural, inclusion-reversing order on proper, symplectic reductions of $M$ with respect to actions by $P$. This fact underlies the concept of a preferred reduction, denoted as $M//P$, which represents the maximum reduced manifold in this order. Preferred reductions enjoy several key properties, including being independent of the initial symplectic reduction, and can be viewed as the natural extension of Kähler reductions from the case of complex actions. A notable result showing that every preferred reduction is holomorphic symplectic reduction appears in the literature, however, we demonstrate that this is not generally true by providing the example of a certain solvable group action on the symplectic vector space $V_3$. Moreover, we establish that the property of being holomorphic symplectic reduction is equivalent to the condition that the moment map's zero set forms a divisor of degree two for the embedded variety, which further implies that it must be a hypersurface in the case of irreducible, rational varieties. Finally, we explore the relationship between preferred reductions and the concept of alterations, which leads to the discovery that preferred reductions can be viewed as the process of symplectic alteration, and thus provide proof of the proposed conjecture of Givental, that every proper reduction is an alteration, specifically an alteration of type (1,1). Additionally, we introduce the term symplectic alteration to replace the previous term symplectic alteration of type (1,1), which was suggested by Givental, and demonstrate that it possesses several key properties, including being independent of the marking, and show that it enables an inclusion-reversing order on the reduced varieties, and finally, we demonstrate that preferred reductions are equivalent to the process of symplectic alteration induced by the zero locus of the moment map, which in turn is equivalent to the process of an analytic alteration of degree two, which implies that it is an isomorphism for irreducible, rational varieties. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Score, a numerical measure of the subjective language used in company statements and earnings calls. We contend that previous research, which has largely viewed this score as a reliable indicator of positive or negative word representations, has been misguided. In fact, we show that the polarity score is essentially a linear combination of two distinct aspects: a reflection of the company's linguistic positivity or negativity and a measure of the words' objective frequency. As a result, any correlation observed between this score and positive/negative word representations can be explained by the association with the corresponding frequency distributions. Consequently, we find no evidence to support the existence of a relationship between the polarity score and these representations. Moreover, we demonstrate that word representations learned through supervised learning techniques correlate with the companies' financial outcomes, providing insights into the financial implications of companies' linguistic choices. Notably, we discover an association between the representations of companies with high Loughran-McDonald polarity scores and those that have experienced accounting irregularities, which prior research has largely overlooked. These findings have significant implications for the use of word representations in accounting research and highlight the importance of modeling the frequency distributions of company statements and earnings calls. Additionally, we identify opportunities for future research into the financial consequences of companies' linguistic positivity/negativity. For example, we find that the representations of companies with high polarity scores have lower credit ratings and are more likely to experience M&A activity. Given the freely available dataset of 433 company statements and earnings calls, along with word representations learned through a range of models, our results and conclusions are straightforward to replicate. We hope this work will serve as a foundation for a broader exploration of the complex relationships between company statements and earnings calls and the word representations learned from them. This article presents two additional OFDM-based designs: a single-input OFDM (SISO-OFDM) and a multi-input OFDM (MISO-OFDM) system. Building on the earlier work in Reference 1, these two new systems can be viewed as equivalents of a particular type of baseband processing called wideband waveforming. When using SISO-OFDM, the power and data transfer channels are treated as frequency-selective channels, which leads to a new criterion for optimizing the carrier allocation and power allocation. In contrast, MISO-OFDM systems treat the power and data transfer channels as wideband multi-user channels, enabling simultaneous data transmission to multiple users. This research introduces an advanced method for managing complex boundary problems related to melting and freezing, where a level-set function is combined with an embedded boundary approach. The level-set technique is used to define and manage the interface between phases, while the embedded boundary method handles the integration and gradient calculations within the interface. The method allows for the representation of sharp boundaries and eliminates the need to artificially maintain a thin interface layer, which is particularly beneficial when modeling high-resolution melting problems. The technique has been successfully applied to a wide range of problems, including Stefan problems, phase change material problems, and solidification problems with convection, and has been shown to accurately model melting problems, including those with moving boundaries and phase change phenomena occurring within the boundary layer. The introduced technique provides greater flexibility and improved performance in comparison to alternative methods and has the potential to be highly beneficial for a wide range of modeling tasks. In multiagent competitions, an ideal equilibrium would have all players making logically sound decisions, unaffected by opposite players' random actions. However, conventional models relying on probability overreact to opposing actions. This research introduces a novel framework, centered on rationalizable games, which addresses such competitions and provides a method for identifying the set of all rationalizable equilibria by analyzing the payoffs in relation to action profiles. This framework also enables identification of a unique, fully robust rationalizable equilibrium, although it may incur a loss in the efficiency of the outcome. A key aspect of this research is the derivation of a generalized potential function for games with multiple, distinct best responses. This leads to an iterative procedure for determining the most internally consistent preference profile, leading to a rationalizable equilibrium. This framework and its resulting procedure are demonstrated through examples and discussions of existing competition models. This research on rationalizable games can be seen as an extension of existing work on repeated games and provides a novel perspective on competitions with multiple best responses. It also offers a possible explanation for the prevalence of cooperative outcomes in real-world competitions. This research investigates the spread of diseases within complex networks that incorporate preventive measures, specifically focusing on how networks respond to infection hotspots by temporarily isolating groups of closely connected nodes. By incorporating a dynamic model of network adaptation, our findings reveal that introducing preventive measures can significantly slow the spread of an epidemic, although it also creates the danger of sudden, extensive network collapse. Our results show that a critical threshold exists, beyond which the rapid dissemination of the pathogen leads to the breakdown of the system. Furthermore, we find that this threshold is raised by increasing the frequency with which the network implements preventive measures, but also note that overly frequent responses can lead to the system's destabilization even when the infection rate remains below this critical threshold. Finally, our research highlights the importance of considering both sudden and prolonged responses in network dynamics, as they exhibit distinct effects on the spread of the epidemic. Overall, our study emphasizes the need for balanced response strategies that account for the diverse impacts of preventive measures on complex systems, particularly during and after the peak of an epidemic, when the effects on the network's dynamics can differ markedly. This research has implications for a range of systems that adapt in the face of stress, including financial markets, infrastructure, and biological systems, and provides a new perspective on the interplay between rapid and gradual responses, which can influence the resilience of these systems to invasion by an unwanted element or disease. In our research, we created the MultiTalk Dataset to further understanding of large-scale dialogue systems. This dataset allows our dialogue system, Branchy, to demonstrate its capacity for extensive, tree-like conversations. Unlike previous approaches, Branchy generates responses not only based on historical messages but also according to a rich set of hidden preferences, making it possible to guide conversations through complex topics and multiple sub-threads. By designing Branchy's objective function to match the unique features of each dialogue turn, we were able to demonstrate the distinct advantages of our approach and showcase MultiTalk's versatility as a platform for exploring various dialogue systems. Our findings on MultiTalk have implications for future evaluation methods of large-scale dialogue systems. The code and the MultiTalk Dataset are available at https://github.com/nyu DAL/. The results can be found in the accompanying technical report: arXiv preprint arXiv 2305.04342.

We introduce PyNMax, a Python extension of PyCGRS, an open-source library for
self-consistent $N$-body simulations in altered gravity theories, specifically
conformally coupled scalar field cosmology. PyNMax streamlines the implementation
of modified gravity frameworks by drawing upon the strengths of both PyCGRS and
Gala, another open-source dynamics solver. Our benchmark tests against previous
works on conformally coupled gravity, including $N$-body simulations and weak
field perturbations, show excellent agreement. A key advancement of PyNMax over
PyCGRS is the inclusion of full dark matter dynamics in its core, enabling the
simulation of complex dark matter systems in altered gravity contexts. Our
results for dark matter halos in $\phi$CDM show that these systems follow the same
patterns observed in general relativity, with notable differences appearing at
the massive end of the halo mass function. Our code is particularly well-suited
for exploring exotic gravity theories and we make PyNMax publicly available upon
request. Our sample simulations may be accessed via the CosmSimDB. The code is

A linearized framework for combustion dynamics was developed by treating the flame as an external source of enthalpy and using it to model the reaction of a jet fire to acoustic forcing. Unlike previous approaches, this method disregards the flame's response to local strain and acoustic oscillations, instead focusing on the interaction between the flame and the turbulent flow. To validate the proposed model, it was compared to results from previous studies, and to investigate its limitations, it was applied to analyze the stability of a premixed flame in a direct current flow. Furthermore, this model was utilized to investigate the possibility of controlling a jet fire by directing acoustic forcing at the flame, and it was observed that when the forcing frequency matches the natural convection roll's period, the flame's response can either promote the formation of a stable inner recirculation zone or divert the flame from this configuration, respectively leading to an increase or decrease in flame height. The results obtained agree with previous findings reported by other researchers. The model's applicability was also demonstrated by analyzing the distribution of heat release rates within the jet fire's plume. The relationship between the forcing frequency and the heat release rate's peak location was found to align with the results reported by other researchers, and it was observed that the distribution of the heat release rate fluctuates in phase with the pressure oscillations in the jet fire's plume. The model's potential uses were discussed, and it was suggested that it could be integrated with large eddy simulation models to analyze the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and acoustic forcing in a more comprehensive manner. The model's current limitations, including its inability to account for local strain's effects on the flame and the pressure oscillations' impact on the flow and combustion processes, as well as the need for more detailed analysis of the flame's response to acoustic forcing, were also identified. The model's current version does not incorporate any control strategies for jet fires, but it could be modified to do so, and it was proposed that future research could explore this possibility. We investigate the neutrino interactions with ultralight dark matter (UDM) of a specific mass range, focusing on the most minimal extension to the standard model known as the conventional neutrinoless double beta decay. This process is mediated by an exact neutrino symmetry and is influenced by UDM through a cosmologically-dependent term. By analyzing the effect of this term, we establish boundaries for the UDM mass based on the absence of neutrinoless double beta decay signals in existing experiments. These boundaries are found to be below the UDM cosmological bounds derived from satellite oscillations in the standard big bang nucleosynthesis model. However, when adopting an alternative model of big bang nucleosynthesis, we obtain a wider range for the UDM mass. This more extensive range is found to align with the results obtained from direct UDM detection in astrophysical environments. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the UDM mass and the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude in experiments such as CUPID, GERDA, and MOON. These findings suggest that even if future experiments with higher sensitivities uncover evidence for neutrinoless double beta decay, it may not necessarily imply the breakdown of the light neutrino hypothesis. Instead, it could be influenced by UDM, with implications for cosmological constraints and the potential for direct detection in nearby sources. Given the complexity of this issue, we propose a theoretical framework for future investigations of the interplay between UDM and neutrinoless double beta decay decay in experiments and in the early universe. This framework is characterized by a set of universal parameters that govern both the cosmological and laboratory phenomena of UDM. The interplay between the light neutrino hypothesis and UDM may also have detectable signatures in future satellite missions for big bang nucleosynthesis, large scale structure, and the cosmic microwave background, particularly in the regime relevant to the MOON experiment. The relationship between the light neutrino hypothesis and UDM can be further explored in experiments such as CUPID, GERDA, and in satellite missions for big bang nucleosynthesis, large scale structure, and the cosmic microwave background, with the potential to constrain the light neutrino hypothesis in the future. The interaction between neutrinos and UDM may also lead to effects on the oscillations of neutrinos in the early universe and in matter, which could be relevant for future long-baseline neutrino experiments in the regime relevant to the MOON experiment. Recently, the human genome sequencing project has facilitated the incorporation of genomic data into medical genetics. However, pinpointing the precise functional impact of most identified genetic variants remains challenging. Our research assembled a comprehensive dataset of 18 human trait genome-wide association analysis results and integrated them with comprehensive genomic data sets, encompassing chromatin structure, active histone modification markers, and expression transcripts. We examined the collaborative evidence between these genomic aspects and established associations for each of the 18 human traits. Our investigation into the collective evidence revealed distinct patterns for each trait, with some exhibiting connections to specific genomic elements, while others demonstrated uniformly dispersed ties. Notably, our findings revealed that traits with limited previous research often exhibit more pronounced and complex genomic profiles. Our study highlights the significance of integrative, genome-wide investigation approaches in uncovering patterns and insights that more targeted methods may miss. Moreover, our analysis of a simulated dataset with artificially incorporated associations yielded an approach called "signal decay," which posits that the extent of trait-related genomic alterations is directly proportional to the strength of associated genetic signals. Our results also demonstrate that attributes with large numbers of associated genetic variants often exhibit more varied patterns of genomic association. Our study consisted of 18 analyzed traits, and we make our results publicly accessible for further study. Our approach, known as the "genomic context score," calculates the extent to which the genome of each trait is modified, along with providing interactive visual representations of the results. Our data and tools are available online at http://genomics.pi.i-kuo.com/. Our approach has implications for prioritizing genetically associated variants, studying synthetic effects in genomics, and better understanding the results of genome-wide association investigations. The LHC is poised to explore the fundamental nature of matter and the role of the Higgs field within the Standard Model, with possible discoveries emerging from QCD in the early stages of operation. In this context, the study of minor QCD processes at the LHC, which occur at a rate 10 to 10^5 times lower than common jet production, becomes an exciting area of research. These "minor systems" include rare meson decays such as phi, eta, and eta prime production, as well as rare baryon and quark and gluon substructure within jets. While individual processes may seem insignificant on their own, studying the collective behavior of these "minor" processes across various experiments can reveal valuable information about underlying phenomena, including asymmetry, symmetry breaking, and the Higgs mechanism. In fact, the contribution from the "minor" to the "major" hadronic cross section in the early LHC runs could be comparable to the contribution from electron positron collisions at the energy level of future colliders like the HL-CLAS at Jefferson Lab. In this paper, we outline the potential of "minor systems" at the LHC to reveal novel physics, with particular emphasis on phi, eta, and eta prime production, as well as the study of quark and gluon substructure within jets. We also examine the capabilities of current and future experiments at the LHC, including the ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb detectors, to measure these "minor" processes and explore the relationship between these measurements and those from electron positron collisions. We conclude by discussing potential pathways for "minor system" studies at the LHC, with a focus on the importance of raw data retention policies and the benefits of simultaneous analysis of "minor" and "major" hadronic cross sections. We anticipate that the study of "minor systems" at the LHC will uncover novel physics, with the possibility of discovering new particles, revealing hidden symmetries, and delving deeper into the fundamentals of the Higgs mechanism. We welcome feedback from the community on this proposal and look forward to collaborating with experimental groups at the LHC to explore the physics of "minor systems" further. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of neutron star binaries with long recurrence periods. It is proposed that many such binaries exhibit outbursts only every 20-30 years, equivalent to one outburst every few decades for each source. This theory is challenging to support due to the long period phenomenon characteristic of these sources, which contradicts the established short recurrence periods (typically less than a decade) resulting from neutron star accretion. It is essential to identify sources with known long periods of inactivity and extensive monitoring data to search for outbursts. For a sample of 21 likely low mass X-ray binary candidates within the Galactic Centre, we analysed a decade's worth of Chandra observations for outbursts and determined their recurrence periods. Recurrence periods were calculated using both an empirical approach and machine learning algorithms. The majority of the binaries exhibited short recurrence periods (less than a decade), consistent with their low mass nature. However, there are 3 sources with longer estimated recurrence periods (10-30 years) that could fit the proposed long period phenomenon. For these 3 sources, we also analysed their X-ray variability and found that 2 exibit the phenomenon of prolonged quiescence, adding characterstic evidence for these sources. This research indicates there is a population of neutron star binaries with long recurrence periods and variable quiescence, supporting the need for continued monitoring of these sources for outbursts. It is also essential to re-examine the hypothesis of no outbursts in sources with only a decade or less of data. The proposed population of neutron star binaries with long recurrence periods and variable quiescence also has implications for the estimated population of the Galactic Centre and the characteristic outburst periods for its X-ray binaries. The proposed population size for the Galactic Centre is approximately 200-400, and the distribution of outburst periods for its X-ray binaries is bimodal, with peaks at a decade and a century. It is also possible that some of the long period sources may be pulsating sources rather than transient binaries. The most persistent sources with the longest recurrence periods for outbursts are likely to be found within the central 0.3 parsecs of the Galactic Centre. Interactive dialog systems based on neural networks often prioritize coherence
over diversity in their responses. While interlocutors typically take turns
building on previous conversations, they also engage in more varied exchanges,
such as debating or discussing opposing viewpoints. In this work, we introduce
the Semantic Variety in Conversation (SVC) dataset, featuring human-conducted
conversations about a given topic, some of which present contrasting NLI
intents. Our analysis reveals SVC dialog's unique characteristics and the
difficulty of fully capturing diversity using standard metrics. To evaluate SVC
dialog's diversity, we develop a post-conversation assessment using a modified
NLI framework. Our findings demonstrate that current state-of-the-art dialog
systems produce less diverse responses compared to human interactions. By
investigating SVC through the lens of Section 5, we identify strategies to
boost diversity, demonstrating that both explicit diversity-encouraging
objectives and the presence of contrasting NLI intents are crucial for varied
conversations. Our work is the first to combine the tasks of natural language
inference and dialog generation, presenting a novel problem that highlights the
challenges of current state-of-the-art models in capturing two aspects: the
semantic variety of conversations and the underlying NLI intentions. Our code
and dataset are available at \url{https://github.com/nyu-dl4mt/ccl}.

Massive rotating stars under strong gravity can exhibit instabilities resulting from axisymmetric modes of oscillation, ultimately leading to shedding of mass and producing jets. While this process is observed in some rotating massive stars and black hole binaries, its occurrence is less clear for low-mass stars and brown dwarfs with low surface temperatures. This paper presents a computational study of rotating low-mass stars and brown dwarfs under extreme conditions, focusing on digital models that account for heat, mass movement, and rotation within these objects over time. Using these models, we simulated a range of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs with different temperatures and rotations, analyzing the development of convection, the structure of their cores, and the shedding of mass and its impact on surface features. Our findings show that in all simulated cases, heat and mass movement converged to a stable state, with mass shedding occurring when the rotation rate exceeded a certain limit, depending on the object's mass, composition, and temperature. This result matches previous findings from simpler models, with the added discovery of two previously unidentified modes of mass shedding due to fluctuations in cellular convection. These results also demonstrate that low-temperature objects with strong magnetic fields may exhibit distinct patterns of mass shedding and surface features, and that the objects in our simulation align with observed characteristics of ultracool dwarfs with surface features indicating rapid rotation. This study further suggests that the objects in our sample, including those with shedding jets, could align with the observed population of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs with jets, and that the digital models used here used used can be applied to better understand the development of stars and brown dwarfs in the early universe. The afterglow signals from these phases will be observable in different energy bands, with the signals from the earliest phases being too weak to be detected in some cases. The model also predicts that short-duration GRBs, which occur when a star is compressed from both ends, will not produce detectable afterglow signals. Given two disjoint vertex sets in a simple graph and specified size constraints for each subset, determining the presence of a partition where each subset contains distinct vertices from separate, non-overlapping components of a specified graph structure, can be accomplished in time that scales factorially with the desired component size and linearly with the number of vertices in the graph. This achievement builds upon the foundational discovery of a fixed-time algorithm for identifying isomorphisms within a simple graph and extends it to bipartite divisions. Recently, researchers have become interested in using less conventional environments for future space exploration, such as lunar and Mars surfaces. To adapt to these settings, robots will require multiple legs to achieve stability and reduce the stress caused by movement. Propellant-reduction is another crucial aspect for future long-duration space missions. To this end, researchers are exploring ways to optimize robotic movement within these environments. By utilizing a simplified model of a robot with multiple legs, researchers have found that bipedal robots moving on low-gravity surfaces can exploit the initial acceleration phase to maintain motion. Furthermore, propelling the robot backward can lead to greater stability and reduced stress.
