We define a new property for valued domains, which we call their residues being comprehensive. This property implies quaternary extension property, previously studied by its connections to the quaternary arithmetic. We demonstrate that this new property holds for fields and their power series extensions. Furthermore, we prove that a domain with a well-ordering and a residue map that is continuous has a comprehensive residue map. Additionally, we examine the relationship between this property and the excellent property of domains. Next, we consider the property of a domain's fraction field in a given extension, and we show it has a comprehensive residue map. Then, we investigate the effect of a given extension on a domain's property of having a comprehensive residue map. Finally, we provide an example of a domain whose fraction field has a comprehensive residue map, but the domain itself does not. This example showcases a connection to the recent work by Kikyo and Schickele on the quaternary arithmetic property. All in all, we uncover a connection between the property of a domain having a comprehensive residue map and its power series extensions, specifically showing that these extensions possess this property if their fields do. Moreover, we investigate the relationship between this property and the property of being excellent, and we provide a counterexample to the potential extension of the quaternary arithmetic property to its higher form. All in all, we investigate a property of domains with a complete residue map and examine the effect of a given extension on this property. This investigation is motivated by the recent work of Kikyo and Schickele on the quaternary arithmetic of their power series extensions. Energy efficiency is crucial for enabling continuous, camera-enabled, and audio-enabled always-on video streaming devices. To enhance the energy effectiveness of such devices, a critical strategy is to lower the CPU frequency. However, reducing frequency also accelerates CPU-induced anomalies that cause video streaming to break down. In this work, we suggest a novel framework called HyperDegrade, a set of frequency-throttling techniques tailored to streaming applications, which significantly boosts the energy benefits of CPU frequency reduction. Our findings, obtained from running the framework on a custom, low-frequency ARMv8 CPU, show it can enhance the energy efficiency of popular video streaming services by 3x for FFMPEG and 4x for the Android VideoDecoder, without any performance overhead. Furthermore, HyperDegrade enables frequencies as high as 1.5GHz to support 1080p streaming, extending the valid frequency window by 500MHz. The developer-friendly framework, combinable with various frequency-throttling techniques, is Extensible, allowing easy integration of new streaming workloads. Our research is accompanied by a custom, open-source CPU implementation and a general, open-source streaming efficiency validation framework. The code is available online.

A non-permissive complex is a non-degenerate polyhedron whose vertices represent knots or link components and edges connect components that share a knot or link, with each face being a circle of three vertices indicating a branch point. Unknotting operations on a non-permissive complex that preserve its properties can be used to create an unknotting sequence for the underlying link. Unknotting sequences are essential in various applications, such as identifying invariant properties of links. Our research introduces the concept of non-permissive complexes and associated unknotting procedures, and we demonstrate that they can be utilized to determine whether a self-link of a knot is trivial. Specifically, a particular type of unknotting procedure called the "branching operation" was initially introduced by Gabai in 1987, and we show that repeatedly applying the "branching operation" to a non-permissive complex eventually terminates if the underlying link is composite, and it produces an unknotting sequence if the underlying link is a self-link of a knot. Moreover, we demonstrate that the branching operation can be alternately analyzed in terms of the Kauffman polynomial, and this polynomial decreases by a factor of $4\Delta^2$ with each branching operation. Consequently, there are only a finite number of distinct unknotting sequences for a given link, and they can be found by examining all possible non-permissive complexes of the link, especially those composed of the self-link components of its knots. Our findings imply that the space of self-links of knots is finite, and this fact can be proved alternatively by examining the behavior of the branching operation in the space of reduced biperiodic diagrams. Additionally, we show that the branching operation can be realized through a sequence of Reidemeister moves, and this fact leads to the discovery that the space of self-links of knots is algorithmically searchable. Our research also shows that the branching operation can be applied to welded links, and this leads to an unknotting procedure for the trivial self-link of a knot in the welded context. While federated learning is gaining popularity, security concerns about malicious users participating badly-behaved attacks continue to impede its widespread adoption, especially in sensitive privacy domains. Badly-behaved attacks, such as a man-in-the-middle attack and a privacy-invasion attack, which we introduce a new category of attacks called pragmatic privacy assaults, can be challenging to detect and countermeasure. These attacks can deceive even the most secure protocols like secure aggregation and federated learning with hidden gradients. We examine the implications of these attacks and feasible countermeasures to enhance security and protocol robustness. Furthermore, we discuss possible detection and prevention strategies for these attacks. We demonstrate that pragmatic privacy assaults are effective against various secure protocols by conducting federated learning experiments on datasets including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST. We find that these attacks can significantly reduce model accuracy and that pre-trained models are more vulnerable to these attacks. We propose a new protocol called Privacy-Assured federated learning, which incorporates a robust protocol and a reinforcement learning-based learning framework that can enhance security and protocol robustness. We validate our proposed protocol through experiments on real-world datasets and find that it can greatly enhance the robustness and security of federated learning. We make our code available at https://github.com/yingxiong1994/practical_privacy_attacks.

In our study, we demonstrated how any group representation associated with a permutation group can be constructed using the wreath product model. Specifically, given a set of individual representation functions for a set of elements within a permutation group, we defined a process called the Cartesian partition method to obtain a combined representation function for the entire group. This process involves breaking down the representation functions into subassemblies, combining them in the wreath product format, and we showed that the resulting combined representation function is identical to the one produced directly through the imprimitive wreath product method. Our research delves into the underlying principles and details of this Cartesian partition method, as well as the specific example of the symmetric group S6. Moreover, we established a relationship between the Imprimitive Wreath Product and the Cartesian Partition method, which enables us to interpret the results of our study within the broader context of the Baik, Cho, and Huh's combinatorial specification theorem. Our findings are demonstrated through an illustrative diagram and made accessible via an accompanying computer program. Our work builds upon the foundation established by Baik, Cho, and Huh in their study of the coefficients of the 1-qubit Pauli matrix eigenfunctions, and our results share a common theoretical framework with their combinatorial formula for these coefficients. Our research was inspired by the work of the same authors on the Wreath Product method and the combinatorial properties of the associated permutation group operators. Our results for the S6 case yield the coefficient values for the 1-qubit Hadamard matrix eigenfunctions, whereas the general theory allows us to derive the combinatorial formula for the 2-qubit Pauli matrix eigenfunctions. Our research demonstrates that the wreath product model exhibits a property of additivity with respect to the subsystem partition, and our findings suggest that this property may be a hallmark of the underlying theoretical framework. Our research introduces the concept of the Cartesian product of a permutation group operator, which arises from combining individual operators in the wreath product format, and our findings show that the coefficient values for the 2-qubit Pauli matrix eigenfunctions are determined by the configuration statistics of these Cartesian products. Our results demonstrate that the combinatorial specifications for the coefficient values of the 2-qubit Pauli matrix eigenfunctions can be obtained through the Cartesian product method, and our findings suggest that this method may be applicable to a broader class of functions, including the 1-qubit matrix eigenfunctions. Our prior research used high-resolution radiative transfer simulations based on the MCNP code to generate observed effects of VSI, while this study uses the results from our previous study to create an empirical model incorporating the properties of disks and their substructures. This new model enables the prediction of dust continuum spectra and allows for variations in properties such as the depth of the VSI-driven layer, the turbulence level, and the particle size. It also explores different modes of VSI and reveals that the resulting patterns are robust and share a common characteristic -- the formation of vertical layers with alternating temperature and opacity gradients. Consequently, our model predicts that the SED of a disk exhibiting VSI will exhibit two peak temperatures, leading to the emission of radiation at two distinct wavelengths. Researchers at the Brookhaven National Laboratory have achieved a significant breakthrough in the study of high-density neutron matter by precisely measuring the density of neutron stars at the facility's maximum reachable intensity. This accomplishment allows for a major reduction in the possible range of a mysterious astrophysical constant and yields the most exact measurement to date of a critical neutron star property called "neutron skin thickness". Furthermore, the findings have been incorporated into a global network that includes a notable experiment called the Electric Dipole Moment of Neutron Search, which is seeking a rare particle that could hint at the existence of new fundamental forces beyond the scope of the established particle theory. The results presented here have been published in the Scientific Reports journal volume 10, issue 1, date 24 July 2019. The research was a collaborative effort involving scientists from 87 institutions worldwide. The facility's ability to create high-density neutron matter at the level of its "ground state" has significant implications for both nuclear physics and astronomy, allowing for a deeper understanding of both cosmic objects and the behavior of matter at the absolute highest densities. The measurement of this density has also been compared to that found in the most stable form of matter called "neutron star matter", and the results have been presented at a range of theoretical densities from 5 to 15 times that of normal atomic matter density. The data from the experiment have been used to create precise graphs of the relationship between the density of neutron matter and the distance between its individual particles, known as the "average neutron-neutron interaction length". These graphs have been analyzed to derive a fundamental theoretical property of neutron matter called "asymmetry energy", which has been found to be approximately 19 megaelectronvolts. This research focuses on creating frequency-resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating multiple motion modes to enhance stability. Initially, a general frequency-shift formula is derived and adapted to account for the precise geometry of linear ion arrangements. This frequency shift is then minimized to ensure the gate's resilience, and it is shown that with two motion modes, this shift can be made extremely small, meeting the requirements for precise quantum computations. Additionally, the connection between motion modes and the gate duration is examined to identify a key crossover point, beyond which a particular linear arrangement of ions becomes preferable. This finding implies that, in certain situations, it may be advantageous to use a setup with multiple motion modes in the cavity of a trap, even if it limits the available gate duration. Finally, the potential for incorporating additional motion modes in a trap setup is also explored in the context of two-dimensionally arranged ions. These results demonstrate that carefully designed linear setups can provide robust frequency-stable Molmer-Sorensen gates, offering a practical solution for tackling frequency fluctuations that present a significant challenge for quantum computations.

Scientists have now proposed a novel approach to design a single crystal made of strong and direct Fermi liquids with linked electronic behavior across all spatial dimensions. By combining van der Waals coupled layered rocksalt osmate and graphene-like layers of osmium, they theorize a single crystal with strong and direct Dirac points and a gapped energy spectrum along the c-direction. This hypothetical material would allow for the realization of highly universal electronic behavior, coupled with unusual effects such as the realization of ferromagnetism and superconductivity in the (001) plane, and could be further optimized by introducing misorientation grain boundaries to achieve universal and coupled dimensional behavior. Although this concept seems ideal, it also presents a set of grand challenges that need to be overcome in real-world implementation. If achieved, this single crystal of linked dimensions could serve as an unprecedented platform for achieving highly universal and coupled dimensional behavior and related effects. Given the complexity of this problem, estimating the necessary conditions requires a multidisciplinary approach that spans condensed matter physics, materials science, and chemistry. Recent over-smoothing face alignment techniques have made it more challenging to achieve high-resolution reconstructions. In response to these challenges, a novel end-to-end framework called SADRNet has been developed to perform both 3D face alignment and reconstruction. This framework consists of two distinct face prediction networks working in tandem, each generating a half-face mesh. These networks are designed to work in conjunction, with their outputs combined to form a complete three-dimensional face mesh. The combined output also enables a self-correction mechanism to enhance the robustness of the alignment. Experimental evaluations on extensive datasets such as the AFLW2000-3D, COFW-3D, and FMIS reveal that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both 3D dense alignment and facial point reconstruction, as well as notable improvements in quantitative face reconstruction metrics. With its unique self-correction alignment capability, SADRNet has the potential to contribute broadly, including applications in face morphing and transfer learning. For certain types of inflationary models, including those based on the $\alpha$-attractor framework, this range can be narrow, potentially aligning with the values inferred from gravitational waves. However, the formation of black holes also relies on the termination of the inflationary period, which can be influenced by the specific characteristics of the inflationary model. Notably, certain $\alpha$-attractor models with a single field exhibit an unstable regime of inflation known as eternally chaotic inflation, where the end of inflation is consistently marked by a transition to oscillatory behavior rather than immediate termination. We introduce the concept of a "deepest" vertex in a labeled ordered tree, defined by its leftmost leaf nodes. Our analysis explores the occurrence of these deepest vertices, considering two ordering scenarios. For right-to-left and left-to-right orderings, we determine the probability that a longest leaf branch occurs at a specific height. Building on this, we calculate the probability distribution of the deepest vertex's height. Furthermore, we find the expected height of the deepest vertex and demonstrate that it converges to a finite value for both ordering types. Specifically, for a tree with $n$ nodes, the expected height of the deepest vertex is approximately $2.5\sqrt{n}$ for right-to-left orderings and $2(2n)^{1/3}$ for left-to-right orderings. Our study also examines the relationship between the highest and second-highest leaf branches' heights and proves it follows a geometric distribution with a specific parameter. Lastly, we discuss the implications and potential connections to random walks and branching processes. Our study was initially presented at the 2021 Virtual International Conference on Computational Science, and we highlight some of the conference discussions within this manuscript.

In this process, images of ballots are analyzed to produce a raw count of votes. While the goal of this step is efficient counting, it's also associated with potential errors and inaccuracies. As a result, these counts aren't considered reliable for official purposes. They do, however, offer significant benefits in terms of speed and cost savings in the counting process. Our research aims to explore the sources of these errors and possible solutions to them. We examined earlier attempts to use AI technology to enhance the accuracy of this process. Our study involves developing a custom framework to correct errors in the image-based count of votes. This framework, which we call "CorrectVote," uses a combination of natural language processing and machine learning to identify and fix these errors. Our findings show that this approach can indeed improve the accuracy of the counts. We also explored the feasibility of using this framework for other types of ballots. Our research used a dataset from a real-world election, specifically the 2020 US presidential election in Virginia, as well as a synthetic dataset to test and validate the CorrectVote framework. Our analysis indicates that this approach offers significant benefits in terms of saving time and reducing costs in the counting process. It's also associated with some limitations and challenges, primarily related to the quality of the images used in this process. Our study suggests several possible ways to address these challenges and improve the accuracy of the counts further. A key challenge in decentralized energy systems lies in properly managing energy storage.  On one hand, storage can facilitate the integration of variable renewable energy sources by mitigating fluctuations in energy supply and demand.  On the other hand, it can contribute to supply imbalances in localized markets by aggregating small-scale generation and energy storage units, also known as prosumers, which may have differing time preferences for energy production and consumption.  To address this issue, a common approach involves instructing prosumers to balance their generation and consumption based on their individual time preferences, with the aim of minimizing transaction costs in decentralized markets.  However, this method overlooks the potential benefits of self-optimization by individual storage units, which can also affect the decision-making process of prosumers.  In the research presented here, a new self-planning framework is introduced for decentralized energy storage units that takes into account the time preferences of prosumers, with the goal of minimizing transaction costs and opportunity losses due to self-thermal efficiency and charging/discharging costs.  The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies, with the results showing that cautious self-planning by individual storage units can lead to better social outcomes in decentralized energy markets.  In particular, it is demonstrated that careful self-planning by storage units in prosumers with contrasting time preferences can reduce supply imbalances and enhance the efficiency of these markets.  The potential applications of this research extend to other problems in decentralized systems, including demand response, supply chain management, and traffic signal control.  The proposed self-planning method can be further improved by incorporating uncertainty into the decision-making process, with the aim of exploring this possibility in future research. The model features a two-layer atmosphere and includes options for both fast and slow rotation rates. When the atmosphere rotates quickly, a state of super-rotation emerges, characterized by wind speeds exceeding the speed of sound. As the planet's rotation slows, these winds accelerate before entering a state of geostrophic turbulence, with atmospheric circulation becoming more complex and erratic. The findings show that the relationship between rotation speed and atmospheric stability crucially influences the formation of clouds and atmospheric circulation patterns, with multiple stable states of circulation emerging when the atmosphere's rotation is moderate. Additionally, the model reveals that small changes in atmospheric conditions can lead to the sudden onset of extreme and unstable states of circulation, with multiple equilibrium states of circulation existing side by side in each planet's atmosphere. The model also highlights the crucial role that atmospheric instability plays in shaping cloud patterns and atmospheric circulation, with clouds forming at the boundaries between different circulation regimes. The research demonstrates that the interaction between a planet's and its star's temperature differences, atmospheric composition, and geological characteristics determines a planet's circulation patterns and atmospheric stability, with implications for the search for extraterrestrial life and the study of planetary climates. This paper presents an analysis of the impact of the learning phase duration on the
final performance of a range of ImageNet-sized learning tasks, considering both
traditional supervised learning and data-driven adversarial training methods. Our
investigations reveal that shorter training phases can sometimes yield higher
accuracy levels, a phenomenon we attribute to several key factors, including the
appearance of oscillatory behavior in model performance over time, the positive
effects of warmer initial models, and the importance of model robustness. To
illustrate the practical applications of this insight, we demonstrate how shorter
training phases can be used to achieve higher levels of adversarial robustness on
the CIFAR-100 dataset without increasing memory usage. Our findings also motivate
the design of a new adaptive learning phase duration algorithm called DeepJoule,
which maximizes performance by maintaining a balance between performance and duration
based on a principled understanding of the relationships between models, datasets,
and learning phases. DeepJoule achieves superior performance to fixed-duration
baselines and demonstrates the benefits of adaptive learning phase duration
scheduling in both supervised and adversarial learning settings. Our code is
available at this link https://github.com/DeepLearningAssurance/AdaptiveDuration.

Our investigation focused on the conductance properties of a HgTe gapless quantum well in the quantum hall regime. By varying the width of the quantum well, its energy spectrum evolves from an overfilled state characterized by extensive Landau filling to a state where the valence and conduction bands intersect, resulting in massless Dirac electrons that behave independently in different layers. In this latter state, we observe the formation of zero-bias resonances both above and below the Fermi level within the light and heavy hole valence bands, and the resulting conductance spectrum exhibits both periodic and chaotic patterns as the magnetic field and quantum well width are varied. The degree of chaos correlates with the presence of massless Dirac states and can be influenced by applying an electric field to create a gap in the energy spectrum. The appearance of gapless Dirac states may also occur in other 2D materials with energy spectra similar to that of HgTe, relying on the composition and band structure rather than the width of the quantum well. The occurrence of Dirac states in these materials could provide a platform for quantum computation, utilizing the immune nature of zero-dimensional defects in 2D entangled states. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations can adjust their transmission and reception times flexibly in response to changing traffic conditions. This feature offers greater efficiency and better performance than traditional TDD designs. However, it also introduces new challenges, particularly the increased risk of cross-talk between uplink and downlink transmissions. To take advantage of dynamic TDD, researchers have begun exploring scheduling strategies from a game-theoretical perspective, aiming to take mutual interference and a multi-objective optimization problem head-on. By considering both uplink and downlink transmissions, they hope to take advantage of dynamic TDD while minimizing the impact of mutual interference. In this paper, we outline a framework for dynamic TDD scheduling based on a non-cooperative game, where nodes prioritize their own data transmission rates over others'. This has been shown to lead to a pure Nash Equilibrium, both theoretically and through simulation testing. Moreover, this framework enables operators to make informed decisions about dynamic TDD configurations. Although this research was conducted in the context of 5G networks, its findings are also relevant to older long-term evolution (LTE) systems. This paper's results have been verified through simulation testing, using both small and large-scale networks. To address these issues, we propose a collaborative online framework for improving the reliability of machine learning models. This method involves multiple autonomous agents that utilize a simple, decentralized protocol to rate the trustworthiness of models and prioritize critical learning data. These ratings and data prioritization mechanisms are then aggregated across the network, leading to a robust machine learning model. We validate our proposed approach in a real-world application, namely anomaly detection in smart traffic systems, and compare it to existing multi-agent learning methods that do not account for trust ratings and data prioritization. The results show that our proposed approach leads to a significant improvement in the performance of the machine learning model, both in terms of detection accuracy and robustness. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is introduced for links in a thickened torus. This polynomial demonstrates an intrinsic property, invariance, under a specific type of transformation, and it also satisfies the volume hypothesis conjecture. Additionally, the proposed polynomial can be expressed through the Kauffman bracket skein relation and satisfies specific boundary value conditions. A computational approach to calculate the polynomial for various links is also provided. Word Sense Discrimination (WSD) is a difficult task that requires distinguishing between distinct senses of the same word based on its context. While WSD has been studied for a long time and various approaches have been attempted, achieving high performance still poses a challenge. In this paper, a novel context-gloss enhancement method is presented for improving WSD. Context-gloss refers to the definition or explanation that accompanies a word, and this method leverages gloss information to train a neural network. Specifically, a network is trained to predict the target word's sense given both the context and gloss, and another to predict the gloss from the context and target word. These two tasks are combined using a multi-task learning approach. Furthermore, an aggressive selection method is proposed to create more manageable training sets by eliminating easy instances. Experimental results show that the proposed context-gloss enhancement method delivers high performance on both SemEval 2010 Task 7 and LexMTK WSD datasets. Moreover, a comparison with 12 diverse approaches using 13 different settings demonstrates the method's efficacy. The challenge of B-Sense, a recently introduced dataset for self-training WSD models, is also tackled to demonstrate the method's robustness. The code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/ContextGloss.

Thanks to advancements in natural language processing, it is now possible to accurately execute complex database queries based on natural language statements. However, executing cross-domain queries poses a significant challenge due to the substantial discrepancy in underlying knowledge. Current frameworks struggle to excel in domains far removed from those used to train the model. This paper introduces a novel framework that tackles the difficult task of executing cross-domain queries by introducing a dual-table design, where an additional intermediate table bridges the gap between the original database and a pseudo-target database. This design enables the model to focus on the syntax and semantics of the query, while ignoring issues related to domain specificity. Furthermore, we introduce an additional task that involves inserting values into the intermediate table based on input statements, thereby simplifying the subsequent execution process. The auxiliary task of value insertion is crucial for guiding the model's attention towards essential elements of the statement. This paper is the first to explore the challenge of cross-domain text-to-SQL by incorporating an additional value insertion task. The proposed framework showcases superior performance in comparison to a range of baselines in challenging cross-domain scenarios, as demonstrated by comprehensive evaluation experiments. Code for this work is available at GitHub.

Various response strategies have been developed to counter this vulnerability, including manipulative data edits and tailored attacks. Another significant challenge is the limited understanding of informed attackers, who possess specific knowledge about the data structure and graphical relationships but whose motives and objectives are otherwise unknown. This article delves into the world of differential secrecy within graph-structured information, exploring the connection between a system's security and the privacy of individual data points. It also examines current attack and defense tactics and proposes a framework for attacking and responding to such attacks. Furthermore, it identifies research gaps in this domain. Lastly, it envisions three possible future scenarios in differential secrecy within this context. This article is suitable for readers with a machine-learning background who are interested in privacy and system security. This article was originally published in null.

We've developed a comprehensive quantum hydrodynamic framework to examine interacting Bose gases within a 2D and 3D phase space. Building on previous work, our approach extends the initial phase-space approach by incorporating quantum fluctuations and interactions. This framework leads to a set of quantum hydrodynamic equations with noise sources, and we demonstrate its applicability to describe condensate destruction and onset of motion in a 1D channel as well as beam propagation in a 2D setup and in a 3D cavity. Furthermore, we compare our predictions to existing literature and other numerical methods, and our framework highlights the significance of noise terms even in situations where thermal effects are minimal. Additionally, we analyze the effects of interactions and provide a phase diagram for a harmonic trap. Our phase-space approach also enables us to examine open systems and we find that our results agree with both analytical and numerical solutions to the Heisenberg picture Sine-Gordon model. Moreover, we discuss our findings in the context of atomic and bosonic Josephson junctions. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to other open and closed systems, including those with defects or boundaries, and we anticipate that it will contribute to better understanding and analyzing experimental and numerical data in atomic, condensed matter, and optical systems. Our code is publicly available at [www.github.com/phase-space-QHD].

This groundbreaking finding also highlights the importance of continued research into the properties of this particular interaction, which influences the behavior of neutron and proton pairs in this closed shell nucleus. A novel approach is proposed to create free-breathing, motion-corrected four-dimensional T2-weighted images.  Currently, free-breathing sequences are combined with image reconstruction techniques such as average respiratory phases to produce four-dimensional images.  However, these images are susceptible to patient movement and may not be representative of individual respiratory phases.  A novel method called multi-excitation motion-sensing sensitivity encoding is introduced, combining motion-sensing and sensitivity encoding techniques to produce four-dimensional images.  This method produces a dataset with the same resolution as the reconstructed image, using only a few respiratory phases.  A designed respiratory waveform is then used to correct the phase encoding direction and produce motion-free images.  A study compared the proposed method with conventional average respiratory phase images and motion-free images produced using retrospective gating.  The results showed that the proposed method's image quality was comparable to that of the conventional method, with a significantly shorter scan time.  Further analysis indicated that the proposed method's spatial resolution was maintained at a level comparable to that of the conventional method, with a mean signal-to-noise ratio of 38.6.  The proposed method was then applied to abdominal imaging scans on two different MRI machines, resulting in high-quality four-dimensional images with a scan time of 420 milliseconds.  The raw data from this method offers opportunities for novel image reconstruction techniques that could produce high-quality images from highly compressed data, as demonstrated by applying compressed sensing to the raw data.  The proposed method's flexibility in phase encoding direction allows it to be adapted to various body scanning applications.  The proposed method has the potential to be applied across different MRI machines and provides a versatile framework for novel image reconstruction techniques.  The data from this study have been made available online.  The method's limitations include its inability to produce images in the phase encoding direction, and the presence of artifacts caused by patient movement.  The proposed method could be modified to produce images in the phase encoding direction, and several approaches are available to mitigate the effects of patient movement.  The proposed method offers a versatile and customizable framework for novel image reconstruction techniques, and its potential applications extend across different MRI machines and body scanning applications. In paired-permutation testing, permutations are often examined in pairs to determine if they resemble each other, with the goal of speeding up tests while maintaining accuracy.  However, implementing efficient paired-permutation testing in libraries like scikit-learn's `PermutationTest` can be challenging due to its need for precise permutation pairs.  To address this issue, a new method called `PairedPermutation Examination` (PPE) is proposed, which evaluates paired permutations by examining whether they can be aligned to form an identifiable pattern in a vector.  This method supports both dense and sparse vector formats and can be used to develop custom paired-permutation testing libraries.  To demonstrate the versatility of PPE, a new paired-permutation testing library called `ppec` is introduced, along with a related method called `Permutation Distance` (PD).  Both PPE and PD have been found to outperform existing paired-permutation testing libraries in accuracy, with PPE also being more energy-efficient.  To further illustrate the benefits of PPE, a use case is presented for efficient paired-permutation testing in multiclass classification problems.  The proposed PPE, along with the `ppec` library and the PD method, are available for download at \url{https://github.com/ghassen/ppec}. We discovered that the direction of maximum drag force can be significantly misaligned with the direction of motion, a phenomenon particularly pronounced when the object's surface friction is lower than the surrounding granular surface friction. Furthermore, when the object and the granular material have the same surface friction, the drag force becomes independent of the angle of motion and behaves similarly to drag experienced by a solid plate. Our findings are relevant to understanding the motion of objects within natural environments such as dunes, sandbars, and riverbeds. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow behavior within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Notably, our results also demonstrated that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow initially decreased with increasing transverse momentum before returning to its initial state. Finally, we extracted triangular flow's centrality and beam-charge dependencies from our simulations, which may be useful for future research aims.

Soft tissue volume to surface registration is a common challenge in surgical planning and training. However, creating flexible models that accurately reflect real tissues is often impractical due to model complexity and time constraints. Our novel method adapts a fast volume-to-surface registration technique for use with data-driven finite element models, enabling the integration of biomechanical information into the registration process. This approach leverages a previously developed algorithm to perform an initial alignment, followed by a optimization process that accounts for both biomechanical features and the discrepancy between the surface and volume models. Our method is evaluated using two types of data: abdominal organs from a publicly available database, and a privately acquired colon dataset. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in integrating biomechanical information and its potential to handle more complex, real-world data. Our algorithm was implemented in C++ and MATLAB, and the code is available upon request. Our analysis also highlights potential avenues for improving the method, particularly in addressing issues related to surface mesh density and its impact on colon data. This work was presented at the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging 2023. Human observers excel at determining scene flow by considering corresponding points across stereo images and assessing the consistency of their connections. This intuition inspires a novel approach to flow estimation, distancing itself from traditional methods that rely heavily on matching features between images. In this research, we develop a pioneering metric learning technique called Adversarial Flow Metric Learning (AFML), which creates a distinction between intra- and inter-image point sets based on a learned metric. This distinction enables the construction of a self-guided evaluation framework that assesses the reliability of points and influences a neural network to focus on more credible connections, ultimately producing more accurate scene flow estimates. Experimental results on datasets such as KITTI show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both epicenter error and density score. Moreover, AFML's capability to produce a uniqueness score for each point enables the creation of a uniqueness map that is exceptionally beneficial for various applications in computer vision. The code for AFML is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr96/AFML.

Spiking Neural Networks, which only activate certain elements during specific events, have shown considerable potential in replicating neural processes while also offering significant energy efficiency. This paper introduces a novel SNN called Random Neural, which incorporates a unique random training method to efficiently classify both simple and complex data sets. By processing information in a more serial manner, this model successfully overcomes the challenges associated with traditional SNN learning frameworks. Moreover, it demonstrates superior performance in comparison to established artificial classifiers, all while utilizing significantly less energy. The proposed Random Neural network exhibits a marked improvement in both energy consumption and accuracy when compared to its static digital counterpart. The extensive experimentation conducted on this model highlights its capability to handle real-world classification problems with a large number of inputs. In this research, we examine the internal characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark matter under high temperatures and strong magnetic fields, specifically within aligned quark matter, and compare these features to those of spin-aligned strange quark stars in various magnetic fields. We computed the energy density of spin-aligned strange quark matter at finite temperatures and strong magnetic fields using the mean-field approximation. Our results show that at low temperatures, the energy density exhibits three distinct phases of magnetized spin-aligned strange quark matter: the neutral phase, the neutral ferromagnetic phase, and the charged ferromagnetic phase. Furthermore, we analyzed the phase structure of spin-aligned strange quark stars in the presence of a strong magnetic field and temperature, and found that they can exist in two phases: the neutral charged phase and the charged ferromagnetic phase. Our calculations indicate that the neutral charged phase is stable at low temperatures and moderate magnetic fields, while the charged ferromagnetic phase dominates at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. We also determined the critical temperatures and magnetic fields for the phase transitions between these two phases. Our research suggests that at low temperatures and moderate magnetic fields, spin-aligned strange quark stars with a large baryon number may possess a neutral charged phase and a specific deconfinement phenomenon, and that these results could potentially be verified through future observations of magnetized neutron stars. Our findings are particularly relevant for the X-ray satellites eROSITA and ASTROSAT, which will be searching for high temperature and strong magnetic fields in close binary neutron star systems. Our work could also be expanded to investigate the effects of strong magnetic fields on strange quark stars in rotating neutron star binaries, and the influence of these fields on the gravitational waves emitted by these systems. Beckwith transformed the concept of the ideal matching number from a geometric metric to a categorical definition within graph theory. This paper introduces a new security solution called Timeloops, aimed at preventing malicious data leaks in containerized applications. It achieves this by limiting access to system calls for individual microservices based on a centralized policy framework. However, the key feature of Timeloops is its autonomous capability to create and manage these policies, without requiring manual input. It does this by analyzing the data that each microservice should be operating with, and comparing it to the data each service has access to through the system calls. If a mismatch is detected, the policy is updated accordingly. Moreover, Timeloops is designed to adapt to the evolution of applications over time, without needing manual intervention. It does this by maintaining a historical record of system calls and using it to update the policies accordingly. The results of our evaluation show that Timeloops is not only highly effective in preventing data leaks but also very efficient in terms of computational resources. Furthermore, it detects policy breaches and learns appropriate system call policies for complex applications like Apache Spark and a proxy server combining multiple microservices. The system is also open-source, with the code available on GitHub. The evaluation also included a comparison with another similar solution called OciGate, which is specifically designed to prevent data leaks in Oracle-related applications. The results showed that Timeloops is not only more scalable but also more secure, with a lower false positive rate for data leaks. This new model extends the basic PMM filter by allowing the initial state to follow a piecewise Markov chain, which can be represented on a grid. This extension provides more flexibility in modeling initial states and can handle circular or non-regular renewal processes. We investigated the performance of the new filter algorithm and found it to be more efficient than the basic PMM filter, especially when the grid-based model is a good representation of the initial state process. Furthermore, we applied this filter to a target tracking problem with mobile sensors, which were themselves subject to movement and delay. This resulted in more accurate and longer-lasting track histories compared to the basic PMM filter. The new filter also demonstrated its effectiveness in other scenarios, including with different sensor configurations and with target models that incorporate acceleration processes. In soccer, players must make intelligent decisions under uncertainty to outmaneuver opponents. Current research focuses on modeling basic game scenarios, but real-life soccer involves complex situations with multiple moving parts. Our work addresses this limitation by creating a deep reinforcement learning framework that allows players to make informed decisions in highly dynamic, large-field soccer scenarios. By leveraging a spatial agent-based model that simulates game dynamics and player movements, our system generates a continuous observation space that represents the position and behavior of players and the ball. We train our policy network to make predictions based on this high-dimensional observation space, resulting in a robust capacity to generalize to unprecedented game scenarios. Experimental evaluations show that our system excels at generating optimal strategies in both simple and complex soccer scenarios, even when faced with unexpected opponent actions. Although our framework succeeds in replicating real soccer scenarios, it falls short of truly authentic representation, as it lacks key elements like goalposts and penalties. To make the system more scalable and harder to solve, we introduced a timing mechanism that forces players to score within a set period. Our findings are further validated by engaging a professional soccer coach in the game. The developed framework serves as a starting point for more sophisticated soccer models, offering potential applications in related problems like multi-agent combat or traffic dynamics. Seismic data interpolation methods can enhance data coverage; however, these techniques alter the initial data configuration, affecting the accuracy of subsequent seismic imaging processes. Separate studies have been conducted on seismic data interpolation and waveform inversion, yet no research has been found that combines the two in a time-domain amplified source waveform inversion framework. This study aims to initiate the development of an integrated time-domain amplified source waveform inversion method by exploring a simple and naive time-domain full waveform inversion strategy. This approach assumes a linear relationship between the source and recorded data and attempts to directly recover the source wavefield through data misfit minimization. Although this method does not recover the actual source wavefield but rather an estimated one, it does so by applying a time-domain full waveform inversion framework. A simulated numerical example serves to evaluate this naive time-domain full waveform inversion method and provides a starting point for further development of an integrated time-domain amplified source waveform inversion framework. Such an integrated framework has the potential to accurately recover missing seismic data and enhance imaging results by directly utilizing the recorded data without the need for separate data interpolation and inversion processes. Future studies could build upon this foundation by incorporating more advanced time-domain full waveform inversion techniques and investigating this integrated framework's performance on real-world data sets. Ultimately, successful development of this integrated framework will contribute to more accurate seismic imaging and better recovery of missing seismic data.

A single-point LDV system is commonly employed for temperature measurements in combustion engines. This paper describes the development of a 2D distance-control method for LDV systems, enabling the collection of 2D velocity measurements in large-scale applications where the object of interest is distant from the LDV system. A key feature of this method is the incorporation of a phase-shifting technique to determine the convection time it takes for combustion-related vibrations to travel from the object of interest to the LDV system, located at a distance. This convection time is found to be 1.4 microseconds in the experiments conducted. A 2D distance-control algorithm is then developed to accurately calculate the distance between the object and the LDV system. Validation of the algorithm is achieved through comparison with the convection time obtained using the phase-shifting technique. Furthermore, a correction is applied to the phase-shifting technique's convection time calculation to account for the LDV system's sampling interval. The accuracy of the 2D distance-control method is assessed in a controlled environment, both with a solid wall and in an engine combustion chamber, demonstrating the feasibility of this method for determining the distance between a LDV system and the object of interest. The method's limitations are also discussed, with the potential issue of time-domain aliasing mentioned. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for improving the method, particularly in regards to the time-domain aliasing problem and the application of this method to multi-point LDV systems. The effectiveness of a programmable phase disk in the transmission electron microscope (TEM) can be evaluated by analyzing the instrument's transfer function to determine if it's possible to correct spherical aberration. To this end, we derived the transfer function of a TEM using the weak amplitude contrast approximation, revealing that the phase disk's impact on the electron wave function is equivalent to a complex conjugate of the specimen intensity. By taking the square of the absolute value of the phase disk, we obtain the instrumental intensity transfer distribution, which can be compared to the ideal distribution for a coherent darkfield imaging technique. The results demonstrate that it is feasible to correct spherical aberration by designing a suitable phase disk, with the possibility of choosing from an infinite set of options. Furthermore, this approach can be combined with overcorrecting and defocusing darkfield imaging to correct not only spherical aberration but also astigmatism and curvature. This method's limitations will be discussed, along with the challenge of implementing this idea due to the constraints of real-time TEM control systems. The possibility of this technique's extension to other instruments, such as scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), is also examined. The findings are validated through numerical computations and experimental measurements, with the latter involving the use of a custom-made test sample to determine the phase disk required for correcting spherical and astigmatism aberrations in the TEM. The results of this investigation have been visually presented in the form of animated GIF images, along with the raw data available for further reference. The code for deriving the transfer function and determining the optimal phase disk is also provided. The discovery presented in this study offers a new perspective on the theory of coherent darkfield imaging and provides a useful tool for users of TEM instruments. A distinctive neural development pattern called interkinetic nuclear migration shapes the cerebral cortex and other pseudostratified neural tissues by creating distinct cell layers. This process involves cells moving towards the surface of the developing brain during cell division and returning to the bottom of the neuroepithelial layer between divisions. Research on this phenomenon is typically limited to static two-dimensional tissue cross-sections, which may not accurately represent its underlying dynamics. To address this limitation, the authors of this study used high-speed light microscopy to observe interkinetic nuclear migration in the developing zebrafish retina in three dimensions. Analyzing this 3D data, they found that this migration pattern is actually random and chaotic in nature, which has significant implications for its underlying biological mechanisms and cell behavior. Furthermore, their findings suggest that this phenomenon can be predicted at a cellular level using a mathematical model called a random walk, which may be applicable to other developing tissues exhibiting this pattern of cell migration. Suggesting that this phenomenon serves a purpose such as maintaining cellular diversity and preventing the formation of the retina's cell layers through premature cell differentiation, rather than solely determining the location of new cell layers relative to the surface of the retina. Recently introduced compressive sensing techniques have been successfully applied in image demosaicing and video compression. In these applications, knowing the sensing pattern can significantly improve performance. This research explores the feasibility of learning a decoder that identifies the sensing pattern associated with each sample, essential for compressive video retrieval. A novel approach called the decoder's understanding of codes (DUC) is proposed, where the decoder learns the sensing pattern's characteristics to differentiate between compressively measured samples. The proposed DUC framework can be integrated with existing algorithms for image demosaicing and compressive video reconstruction. Experimental results in compressive video retrieval demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework, showing a 6 dB improvement in PSNR over a baseline approach. Similarly, the DUC framework leads to a 5 dB PSNR gain in image demosaicing under certain sensitivity levels. The proposed framework's effectiveness is further validated through the compression of still images, demonstrating a 2 dB PSNR improvement over a baseline approach. The DUC framework's potential is also presented through the incorporation of DUC with existing algorithms for image demosaicing and compressive video reconstruction. This work focuses on the basic model, without additive noise, and introduces a novel combinatorial argument to overcome the previous obstacle limiting $d$ to $2$. By analyzing the interaction between polar particles, we show that there exists a critical density $\phi_c$, such that polar clusters can coexist stably in the state of matter known as jamming, where $\phi_c$ is directly influenced by the characteristics of the random environment. Furthermore, we demonstrate that below this critical density, polar clusters can become arbitrarily large, with $N$ particles being able to form $k$ independent clusters with sizes driven by the laws $L_{\rm big}\sim t^{\beta}$ and $L_{\rm small}\sim (\log t)^{1/\theta}$ for $d=3$, and $L_{\rm small}\sim t^{1/d}$ for $d>3$, where $d=3$ the exponent $\beta$ equals $1/3$, and for $d>3$ it equals $1-(\gamma_{\rm per}/d)$, with $\gamma_{\rm per}$ being the exponent characterizing the stability of the hypercube percolation, where $\phi_c$ and $\gamma_{\rm per}$ are fixed at $\phi_c=\frac{d^{2}-1}{d^{3}}$ and $\gamma_{\rm per}=\frac{3}{2}$ for $d=3$, and $\phi_c=\frac{2}{d}\left(\frac{d-1){d-2}\right)^{d-2}$ and $\gamma_{\rm per}=\frac{2}{d-2}$ for $d>3$. To assess the impact of external driving forces on quantum harmonic oscillators in thermal equilibrium, we developed an analytical approach and alternative Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCC) methods to investigate the driven oscillator's dynamics. Our analytical solution for the driven oscillator's expectation values of energy and position includes a series of graphical representation tools, illustrating the effects of driving forces, temperature, and amplitude on the particle's dynamics. Alternatively, we employed the path integral formalism to describe the driven oscillator, with Monte Carlo integration methods providing an independent means of calculating the same dynamical quantities. Our results for the energy and position probability distributions from the two methods converge, validating our path integral Monte Carlo approach. We also investigated the driven oscillator's dynamics using three distinct Monte Carlo integration methods: Metropolis, Multilevel Monte Carlo, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. While all methods yield comparable and consistent results for the driven oscillator's dynamics, each has its own advantages and requires a distinct computational effort to achieve the same level of statistical convergence for the same quantity of interest. To further explore the driver-activated harmonic oscillator's dynamics, we used our analytical solution to investigate the effects of driving forces on the particle's energy and position distributions as the temperature and amplitude of driving change. We found that driving forces force the particle to occupy higher energy states and shift the peak of the energy distribution accordingly. In contrast, the probability distribution of the particle's position remains Gaussian and its peak shifts in response to changes in driving amplitude, but remains unaffected by changes in temperature. We also introduced a new measure that reflects the particle's energy-activated state and used it to demonstrate that driving forces create a energy distribution that is bistable or oscillates in response to changes in temperature or driving amplitude. In the latter case, this behavior is characterized by a periodic variation of the energy distribution's average energy, with the peak of the distribution aligning with the central minimum of the parabola that defines the particle's energy spectrum. In this scenario, the driving amplitude needs to exceed a certain threshold to initiate this behavior, with the particle's energy distribution becoming pinned to one of the two available states for driving amplitudes that are less than half of the required threshold. For driving amplitudes greater than half of the required threshold, the particle's energy distribution becomes bistable, with the particle's energy fluctuating between the two available states as the temperature changes. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by causing a net torque that results from solar and planetary radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface of these objects. As a result of this effect, the rotation period of an asteroid can either speed up or slow down over time. The YORP effect has a substantial impact on the stability of certain rotation states and can lead to the formation of unusual rotation periods, especially those that are commensurate with the orbital period of a planet. The YORP parameter, which characterizes the YORP effect for an individual asteroid, depends on the reflectivity and thermal properties of its surface. The YORP effect also competes with other influences that can shape the rotation of an asteroid, such as gravitational tidal interactions with a planet or a binary companion, and that result in a stable rotation period. In this study, we examine the influence of the YORP effect on three small asteroids with measured rotation periods: (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos. The reflectivity and thermal properties of these asteroids' surfaces were determined by analyzing infrared observations of the asteroids. We calculated their YORP parameters and examined how the YORP effect interacts with other forces that shape their rotation periods. The YORP effect is strong enough to drive the rotation period of (10115) 1992 SK to continue speeding up, while it slowed down in the recent past. The reflectivity of (1685) Toro's surface is highly anisotropic, resulting from its elongated shape, which causes a particularly large YORP effect for this asteroid. The YORP effect is strong enough to drive the rotation period of (1620) Geographos to continue speeding up in the recent past. The study also offers a group-theoretical characterization of the property in question and leverages this to prove that groups with a specific subgroup characteristic are non-Roelcke precompact. We introduce a new framework for discrete operations on infinite strings, which we call regular operations, and show that any function from infinite strings to infinite strings that can be computed by a Turing machine with a finite number of heads, also computes a regular operation. Furthermore, we establish that there are computable regular operations that are not uniform over infinite strings, providing a negative answer to a problem posed by Khoussainov and Wang. Additionally, we offer a characterization of computable regular operations in terms of monadic second-order logic, and demonstrate that this logics is stronger than monadic logic with transitive closure. Moreover, we identify a natural problem that is decidable using regular operations but undecidable using the more general framework of partial functions from infinite strings. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between our results and those of Caucal who examined operations on infinite trees. All of our main results appeared in a prior paper but the current version includes an additional theorem not present before. The research described here was conducted by the first author alone. For isotropic and anisotropic systems with interacting particles, the behavior of a single particle can be significantly affected by the surrounding environment. In particular, the motion of a particle in a crowd can be either slowed down or sped up due to interactions with other particles, which are classified as obstacles or coexisting particles. While the effect of other particles slowing down a particle is well understood, there's a lack of knowledge about the effect of other particles speeding up a particle, especially in random, disordered systems with coexisting particles. In this study, we examine the motion of a particle in random, two-dimensional systems with long-range interactions between particles. With the help of computer simulations, we investigated various systems, including crowded systems with both coexisting particles that slow down and those that speed up a particle. Our results show that the effect of coexisting particles that speed up a particle is more complex and varied than expected. Notably, we found that systems with a high density of particles that speed up a particle can behave similarly to systems with a high density of obstacles. However, by analyzing the distribution of the slowing-down effect, we were able to distinguish between these two systems. Our findings have important implications for the non-equilibrium dynamics of crowded and systems with long-range interactions between particles. Moreover, we believe that the approach we used to analyze the data can be applied to other, related problems. Finally, our results highlight that the behavior of a single particle in a crowd is highly unpredictable and cannot be determined based on the average interaction between particles and the environment. In addition, we discovered that the distribution of the slowing-down effect is non-Gaussian and varies significantly from one simulation to another. This non-Gaussian distribution creates a significant barrier for statistical measurements that rely on linear expansions. To overcome this challenge, we developed a non-linear expansion known as the cumulant expansion method. With the help of this method, we were able to accurately measure the average effect of coexisting particles that slow down a particle and the dispersion of this average effect. Furthermore, we found that the average effect of coexisting particles that slow down a particle and the dispersion of this average effect remain constant over time in our simulations. In contrast, the average time a particle spends in a state where it is sped up by other particles fluctuates more significantly. Recently, the first-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation has gained popularity as a viable approach to determining achievable sets for dynamic systems under constraints and uncertainties. However, its second-order counterpart, which would provide a more accurate solution, has been challenging to solve due to its complex nature. Building on the foundation of the HJI formulation, we introduce a novel Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs-Sengupta (HJIS) equation, incorporating a Cauchy-type variation, which enables the computation of second-order achievable sets. We demonstrate the superiority of the HJIS framework by showing that it can be reformulated to resemble the HJI formulation, which can also determine first-order solutions for comparison purposes. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm to numerically solve the HJIS equation, and our results are accompanied by a tangible dynamic domain inference example. This example, involving a double integrator system with input and state constraints, serves as a tangible demonstration of our method's effectiveness, which is also compared against the HJI-based approach for added context. The human ventral temporal cortex, particularly the region known as the animacy sensitive area (ASA), is distinguished by its exceptional sensitivity to the classification of living versus non-living entities. Research suggests a unified representation across the ASA for basic categorizations of living and non-living things. However, the animacy structure theory proposes a more complex framework, consisting of multiple layers that distinguish between different types of living beings based on their level of animacy, such as distinguishing animals from plants. A recent study found evidence to corroborate the animacy structure hypothesis, revealing a hierarchical organization in the ASA where more primitive life forms, such as plants, are separated from more complex life forms, such as animals and humans. A key finding showed that the distinction between animals and plants is evident in a deeper layer of the ASA than the distinction between living and non-living entities. A further analysis revealed that the region that differentiates animals from plants also differentiates humans from these other two categories, suggesting a representation that prioritizes the level of biological complexity within the animal kingdom. A discussion on the implications of this discovery for the study of the ventral temporal cortex and the nature of its representation is presented. Additionally, this statistical behavior is shown to be shared by the roots of polynomials arising from the Siegel's zeros of L-functions. These findings are further generalized to extend the principle of quantum unique ergodicity to measures generated by higher degree Hecke eigenforms within a specified context. The research also leverages recent advances in the study of Hecke eigenforms and the connection between Dirichlet series and analytic properties of L-functions. The assumed condition of analytic continuation in the right half-plane for the associated Dirichlet series can be swapped for the condition of complete zero-free region for the associated L-function, thereby broadening the underlying scenario. The results presented are shown to hold for measures generated by measures associated with higher degree Hecke eigenforms, as well as Landau-Siegel roots, within a specified context where the underlying L-function has a specified distribution of zeros, namely the distribution of zeros occurring in the left half-plane. The occurrence of quantum unique ergodicity for these measures is further demonstrated to imply the non-existence of Landau-Siegel zeros or the absence of zeros in the left half-plane, depending on the specific context in which the results hold. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases often relies on a single individual with intense connectivity, who possesses an exceptionally broad social network. This theory, known as the "power law tail," has significant implications for the speed of disease spread. To examine this concept further, we introduce a new epidemiological model based on the configuration model, which allows us to explore the effects of highly connected individuals on epidemic progression. This model reveals that a small group of super-spreaders, who are highly connected to the rest of the population, can significantly contribute to the rapid spread of a disease. In fact, the model shows that a few super-spreaders can cause a pandemic to spread many orders of magnitude faster than would be possible in a random network of the same size. This accelerated spread is further exacerbated when these super-spreaders are highly connected to each other, as it creates a critical mass that can drive a epidemic to an outbreak. This model also reveals that targeting these super-spreaders for vaccination may not always be the most effective strategy in reducing the spread of a disease. In particular, it shows that if these super-spreaders are highly connected to each other, it may be more difficult to contain the epidemic through vaccination, as it requires a higher number of vaccinated individuals. This finding highlights the importance of considering the complex structure of a network in understanding and controlling the spread of a disease. This model can be applied to examine the transmission dynamics of infectious diseases in networks that feature power law degree distributions. This is because its focus on the most connected individuals in a network makes it particularly well suited for this purpose. This model can be used to investigate various aspects of disease transmission dynamics, including the critical vaccination coverage required to prevent an epidemic from breaking out, the number of new cases that an epidemic can cause, the duration of an epidemic, and the probability of an epidemic occurring in the first place. This is achieved by analyzing a susceptible-infected-recovered model on a network with power law degree distributions, which provides a more accurate representation of many real-world networks than traditional random network models. This model has been tested on a variety of networks with power law degree distributions, including academic collaboration networks, air transportation networks, and protein-protein interaction networks. This includes a large dataset of 1,446 real networks with power law degree distributions, which were analyzed to examine the effect of power law degree distributions on disease transmission dynamics. This has significant implications for various fields, including epidemiology, sociology, biology, and finance, which often involve complex networks with power law degree

The accuracy of solar vector magnetometry is dependent on precise measurements of Stokes parameters, which can be inferred using imaging techniques such as spectrography. However, such measurements may contain varying levels of accuracy and bias across different observations. While some data shows a consistent degree of bias across all measurements, others exhibit it only in specific heliometric regions. To account for these observed biases, researchers modify the inference process by incorporating additional terms that vary by both observation and heliometric coordinates. This approach is particularly effective in analyzing local phenomena, such as flux emergence and fragmentation, that occur in specific regions of the sun. Furthermore, considering the finite resolution of magnetometry techniques, researchers must also take into account the effects of spatial noise on measurements and corrections for bias. By applying these modifications to simulations and actual data, the resulting vector magnetometry data show significant improvements, particularly in areas with intense magnetic field patterns. These findings suggest that the proposed model, combined with advanced preprocessing techniques for Stokes measurements, can significantly enhance the effectiveness of vector magnetometry in analyzing complex solar phenomena. This research was conducted as part of the SUNRISE mission planning and has implications for similar vector magnetometry missions in the future.

A key challenge in developing efficient and accurate neural approximations lies in addressing the "sign dilemma," a complex issue arising from the quadratic term in the Taylor expansion of the logarithmic function. This problem has significant implications, especially in physics-based research, where it limits the use of powerful neural tools, such as complex-weight neural networks, that are otherwise necessary for simulating many-body interactions accurately. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based framework known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled data to locate relevant examples that facilitate the model's discovery of new patterns and rule-based behavior.
The proposed framework incorporates two innovative techniques: a semi-supervised preprocessing step called precursor retrieval, which prepares the dataset for finding successor instances with desired properties; and a novel evaluation metric called the intrinsic zero-shot transfer score.
Our experiments on both T0 and FLAN show significant improvements in cross-task generalization, with outcomes on challenging real-world datasets like the GEM dataset revealing substantial gains in both supervised and unsupervised settings. The code for ReCross is publicly accessible at https://github.com/THUDM/ReCross. The proposed framework provides a versatile platform for exploring various precursors and successor instances with different property definitions, thereby offering valuable insights into the underlying mechanics of large language models. The future potential of ReCross for addressing complex problems like multi-step reasoning and adversarial attacks is also discussed. Ensuring user data privacy is increasingly crucial for modeling using large datasets. The privacy risks associated with publishing sensitive information, such as health data and personal details, necessitate the use of differential privacy methods. Although differential privacy provides robust protection against user data, it incurs a significant computational cost and degrades model performance. This study highlights the challenges of tuning hyperparameters under differential privacy constraints and demonstrates a practical approach to reduce private learning's computational burden. We propose a simple yet efficient hyperparameter tuning strategy called 'Grid Search Rejuvenation.' This approach initially conducts a broad grid search to identify a compact subset of promising hyperparameters. It then performs an in-depth exploration within this reduced set to locate the optimal parameters. Our results show that this two-stage strategy outperforms other hyperparameter tuning methods, both publicly available and previously proposed private learning approaches. To support our findings, we present an empirical analysis of grid search rejuvenation, highlighting its advantages in reducing the private learning pipeline's computational burden without compromising model performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/abhishek3210/hprtdp. Our findings have implications for practicing researchers and engineers working with real-world datasets in private deep learning settings. Our approach prioritizes efficient hyperparameter tuning to reduce the computational burden of private learning without degrading the model's performance.
