A significant subset of these groups are known as right-angled groups. They have a distinct property where their subgroups are naturally associated with the subgroups of the group formed from the graph's flag complex. In this paper, we investigate the group defined by an equilateral triangle graph and demonstrate that it possesses a specific kind of subgroup structure called a division, which cannot be found in any right-angled group. This discovery provides a concrete answer to an open problem posed by the first author. Moreover, our findings reveal that the triangle group's subgroups do not form a free monoid, which also addresses another unresolved problem. Finally, our research on triangle groups also reveals that they exhibit another property called a standard presentation, which differs from the standard definition typically associated with the term. This distinct presentation property of triangle groups is investigated in the paper's appendix. Ultimately, our results on triangle groups with an irregular triangle graph can be generalized to groups defined by any graph containing a triangle as a subgraph, leading to the term right-angled groups with a triangular defect. These generalized groups preserve the property of their subgroups associated with the flag complex, providing an intriguing class of groups with which further research is warranted. The paper's final section is devoted to presenting two conjectures regarding these generalized triangle groups. The first conjecture proposes that the free monoid structure associated with these groups can be achieved at the level of their subgroups formed from the graph's line complex, rather than the flag complex. The second conjecture suggests that the standard presentation property is actually a defining feature of these groups, which could then be referred to as standard groups. Identifying complex connections across interconnected systems, whether in finance, biology, or physics, is a recurring problem. Connected systems can exhibit periodic, random, or controlled behavior, and connections may unfold instantly or take time. A new method, Dynamic Graph Attention Network (DGAN), is presented for automatically discovering these connections and uncovering the underlying graphs from multivariate time series data. In contrast to conventional approaches that rely on fixed attention mechanisms or graphical models, DGAN utilizes neural networks with flexible learning capabilities to determine both instantaneous and temporal connections. The effectiveness of DGAN is demonstrated across distinct tasks, including efficient time series forecasting, anomaly detection in financial data, and connectivity estimation, using real-world datasets including the Amazon traffic data, stock prices, and brain signal recordings. Experimental results show that DGAN outperforms existing methods in many cases, offering a versatile tool suitable for a broad range of applications involving interconnected systems. The code for DGAN is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Dynamic-Graph-Attention-Network.

The concept of trims, a generalization of roots, is introduced for finite group presentations. It is shown that two groups with isomorphic universal covering groups are shown to have isomorphic subgroups generated by the same set of generators, where the relation defining the universal covering group can be any set of relations including the ones formed by the trims of the given group. A direct application of this result to the finite group F_29 proves that the group has a specific order, precisely 2^19*3^5*5^2*7*11*13*17*19. A significant challenge in identifying the Higgs boson in particle collision data lies in distinguishing neutral Higgs bosons from multiple sources, particularly in experiments like the LHC, due to varying scattering processes and massive particle combinations. As particle energies increase, it becomes essential to prioritize on-shell Higgs production predictions, particularly for $b\bar{b}$ decays, which are more reliable and less affected by theoretical uncertainties. In the context of the Minimal Superoxymetry Standard Model, on-shell Higgs production predictions for $t\bar{t}$ and other multi-body final states, such as $t\to t + H$ decays within stop physics, are particularly relevant. Here, we examine the influence of intricate stop parameters on on-shell Higgs production in the Minimal Superoxymetry Standard Model, highlighting complex phenomena such as light stops with large mass splittings and mixed Higgs-joint states within the stop sector. These intricate situations often result in distinctive on-shell Higgs signals that may help in identifying stop physics and its implications for supersymmetry. This study emphasizes the significance of precisely measuring $t\bar{t}$ scattering and stop decay modes at future LHC runs with higher energies and better detectors. Contextual decision-making involves making choices that depend on individual-specific contexts, and linear gambit theory provides a framework for this by positing that context-dependent values follow a linear relationship. This work explores a decentralized learning scenario where agents make decisions based on private contexts and try to infer the underlying linear context-dependent values. It is assumed that decision-making histories are observable, and the focus is on determining the rate at which the sum of agents' value estimates converges to the true values. It is shown that this convergence rate can be upper and lower bounded by a square root of the number of actions chosen, and various robustness and distributional extensions are also examined. Furthermore, a data-driven approach to estimating the optimal sample size for accurate value estimation is proposed and analyzed. Finally, simulations and an empirical study on cricket batting scores are presented to illustrate the results. This work was previously known under the title "Decentralized Learning in Contextual Linear Gambits".

A simulation framework for complex fluid interactions, particularly with regard to particle interactions, needs a collision resolution method that balances speed and accuracy. While fast methods like the direct numerical simulation of collisions are accurate but time-consuming, alternative approaches like the fast convergence method mentioned here resolve interactions more quickly while maintaining the speed of the simulation. This approach determines the duration of a collision based on its type, either treating it as a instantaneous event or simulating it over several time steps, which can range from.01 to 100 time steps, depending on the scenario. This research applies this method to multi-step collisions in particulate flows, demonstrating its effectiveness by simulating the flow of various fluids with different particles, including solid particles, bubbles, and drops, and compares the results to the traditional method of simulating collisions over many time steps. The data shows that this approach not only accelerates simulations by 2-5 times but also yields similar and sometimes improved accuracy, making it a superior option for large-scale simulations. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This unified framework is particularly beneficial for the study of heavy mesons, where the contribution of quark masses cannot be disregarded, and it offers a more intuitive understanding of the results for the 'radius' of heavy mesons. Quantum annealing has seen significant development, and is now applied to a variety of problems, but its success rate in finding the ground state remains a challenge. Research suggests that this difficulty could be alleviated by controlling the quantum annealing interval, allowing for the systematic development of efficient quantum algorithms. In this study, we investigate the implications of variable quantum annealing intervals on the quantum success probability for exact cover problems. Introducing the quantum acceptance ratio curve, we show that the region below a specified threshold curve determines the quantum success probability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this curve can be obtained pre-processor, facilitating efficient parameter tuning. Additionally, we discuss the connection between the quantum acceptance ratio curve and quench dynamics, which provides insights into quantum barrier tuning and offers the potential to expand the quantum success region. Our research highlights the potential of quantum annealing to excel in exact cover problems, and our pre-processor-based protocol is likely to yield comparable performance for other combinatorial optimization problems. Although this protocol may not yield the ground state with high probability, it significantly enhances the quantum success probability for a given experimental failure count. Our data is obtained using the D-Wave 2000Q quantum annealer. This study sheds light on the uncontrolled elements of quantum annealing experiments, and suggests that better success probabilities may be achievable with the current technology by employing suitable annealing intervals. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlexKrasnov/Quantum-Annealing-Intervals. To effectively address the challenging open-domain Commonsense Question Answering task, we introduce an innovative approach, C2P, which tackles the problem from a reverse perspective. Beginning with a precise answer, our method navigates towards a coarse semantic understanding. We incorporate a novel semantic-related distance metric, averaging thematic and operational distance components, to guide this journey. This approach enables us to leverage multiple sources of information, integrate diverse knowledge, and discover the underlying connections between questions and answers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, comparing it to alternative strategies, and show that C2P consistently outperforms the baselines in the BAbI dataset evaluation. Furthermore, our method excels when the question-answering pair exhibits a complex relationship, with a notable improvement in the SQuAD v1.1 dataset evaluation. We also examine the influence of different distance metrics and provide a technical implementation of our approach. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our work and potential avenues for further development. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/C2P.

A major challenge in cross-training for federated learning from diverse data is addressing differences in data distribution. Existing methods typically prioritize model aggregation based on dataset contributions, which can lead to bias towards larger datasets and less accurate global performance. Our innovative random stroll method breaks from this tradition by instead focusing on unequal data distributions and using client data statistics to create a diverse set of exploration weights. These weights are designed to guide the model through varied data distributions, allowing it to learn from diverse data without prior knowledge of the data landscape. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data, and our results show that the random stroll method outperforms several baselines in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the optimal model depth and learning rate both converge to expected values as the number of client datasets increases, providing valuable insights into model complexity and data diversity. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruan/Stroll.

Research suggests that participating in mental health treatment during or after their sentence can significantly reduce recidivism and improve overall well-being for this population. Nonetheless, implementing mandatory mental health interventions remains a contentious issue due to concerns about infringement on personal freedoms and potential negative consequences, such as increased resentment towards the justice system. This study examines the relationship between compulsory mental health treatment, general welfare, and future criminal activity by analyzing a comprehensive dataset from the United States. It finds that participating in required mental health services can lead to improved mental health and a decrease in repeat offenses, although the effect on the latter may vary depending on the context. It also discovers that the beneficial effects of such programs on mental health and overall wellness are more pronounced when treatment is provided during the sentence, whereas the impact on reduced rearrest rates is greater with post-release treatment. Nonetheless, even programs with negative consequences for some individuals still appear to exhibit a generally resilient impact on reducing rearrest rates and improving mental health. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper presents a novel technique to utilize partially annotated images for training. A medical image is considered as a superpixel graph, with nodes representing superpixels and edges representing the relationship between them. Each node has an attribute associated with it, either fully annotated or a single control point. The task is then to train a network to minimize the discrepancy between the predicted superpixel labels and the actual annotations. This technique can be viewed as a form of regularization or a way to incorporate unannotated data. Experimentation with brain and pancreas image segmentation shows that this method is effective, outperforming other baselines in many cases. The code for this technique is available open-source.

Quantum complexity manifests as an obstruction to precise long-term predictions in various closed quantum systems, and graph neural networks have successfully demonstrated the capability to accurately model these systems, especially in capturing the intricate dynamics of highly entangled states. However, the underlying causes of quantum complexity, including intense interactions and initial state preparation, have been challenging to identify. Our research introduces a novel graph neural network that not only effectively predicts long-term behavior but also provides insights into the key factors influencing complexity. By applying this framework to a realistic model of a Bose-Einstein condensate subject to periodic perturbations, we found that complexity is significantly increased when the system enters a chaotic regime characterized by random emission of matter waves. Moreover, our network successfully pinpointed the destructive interference between different quantum states as the primary source of this enhanced complexity. Finally, we demonstrate that this framework can be an reliable tool for investigating the interplay between different levels of interactions, initial state preparation, and system size on complexity and chaos. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/QC-NN/Graph-Neural-Chaotic-Dynamics. Our results highlight the potential of graph neural networks not only as predictive models but also as analytical tools for uncovering the underlying mechanisms of closed quantum systems. Our research was featured in the journal Nature Physics.

Multilingual automatic speech recognition systems are beneficial for handling out-of-domain speech. The performance of a massively multilingual model can be enhanced by incorporating a specially trained model for a particular language. We explored the effectiveness of a two-stage transfer learning process, beginning with a massively multilingual model and followed by a target-language model. The research revealed that using a massively multilingual model pre-trained with a large multilingual dataset results in improved speech recognition performance for a less commonly spoken language like Japanese. Additionally, the study examined whether a similar performance gain could be achieved with a model trained in a different language, namely English. Recently, Gaussian Process (GP) models have been successfully applied in navigation domains for modeling robot surroundings and detecting temporal variations. However, GP regression typically carries significant computational and memory costs, which can result in large data storage needs and prolonged inference times. Moreover, current GP-based temporal variation learning methods fail to leverage the sparsity inherent in many real-world environments, including the marine setting under investigation. This research aims to enhance the efficiency of GP-based temporal variation learning and surroundings representation while preserving the benefits of GP model accuracy. We introduce a novel, sparse GP framework, initially representing the environment as a GP before identifying the most significant, non-stationary locations using an information-based criterion. We then focus the GP hyperparameter estimation and prediction on these detected areas, thereby significantly reducing computational costs and memory requirements. The proposed method was evaluated in a marine navigation scenario, yielding superior results in terms of accuracy, memory usage, and inference time in comparison to the existing state-of-the-art GP-based approaches. Moreover, our sparse GP model demonstrated superior performance in comparison to traditional navigation methods, including GP-based, non-sparse alternatives. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/ShuaiXieAUEB/SparseTemporalGP.

We employ a semi-exact method to investigate self-gravitating objects in a dual-fluid model within General Relativity. This model comprises a nonrelativistic fluid undergoing shear stress and a relativistic fluid. By applying a new approximation, we derive an effective semi-relativistic description. For a spherically symmetric configuration, this description yields a set of modified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. We then solve these equations numerically to analyze the properties of the dual-fluid objects. Notably, our approximation reveals that the model can exhibit both isotropic and nonisotropic behavior, and we identify key markers for nonisotropic behavior. Furthermore, we establish that the approximation breaks down at a certain density threshold, where the object becomes highly nonisotropic and a black hole is formed. This result is consistent with previous findings obtained using a different approximation technique. We also examine the effects of shear viscosity and the interaction between the two fluids to demonstrate their impact on the object's isometry. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the objects' properties and their mass and density, uncovering distinct thresholds where the object's behavior changes significantly. This includes the appearance of universal sequences, the onset of nonisotropic behavior, and the formation of a black hole. These findings suggest that the properties of self-gravitating objects depend on the fluid's properties and the interaction between the fluids' components, rather than the specific details of these properties. This conclusion holds true for a much broader class of models, not limited to the dual-fluid scenario. We conclude by outlining potential research paths to explore these findings further. This work is also relevant to condensed matter and nuclear physics, where similar phenomena occur, and we discuss its implications for these fields. Evaluating grammatical errors in languages requires adapting existing datasets, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. To streamline this process, researchers propose a domain adaptation approach using few shot learning, where a compact model is trained to accurately identify errors in new language datasets with minimal data. The proposed framework, called GERRTL, leverages meta-learning to transfer knowledge from initial training data to new domains, facilitating domain adaptation without significant data requirements. Empirical evaluations on publicly available datasets demonstrate that GERRTL outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in five evaluated languages, with an average improvement of 5.67% in exact match accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed approach excels in transferring knowledge between domains with limited data, demonstrating potential utility in tasks like integrating tree-based error annotation tools. The code for GERRTL is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-dl4mt/GERRTL. The proposed framework provides a foundation for developing more efficient error annotation tools and integrates seamlessly with existing methodologies, such as selective annotation and model ensemble methods. Consider a situation in which multiple agents compete to allocate specific items to agents based on their requested quantities, with the items being non-divisible and their total sum exceeding the number of items to be allocated. Assuming agents act selfishly and honestly declare their demands, we can determine the pure Nash equilibria for two key models: one in which items are allocated proportionally to the largest demand for each item, and another in which items are allocated to the highest bidder for each item. We examine the relationship between these equilibria and the existing algorithms that distribute items fairly. Moreover, we investigate the impact of these equilibria on the agents' declared demands, with a focus on maintaining the integrity of declared demands and identifying the agents who are treated fairly in the allocation process. Lastly, we discuss possible extensions to these results for more complex situations in which agents compete to allocate multiple items to multiple agents. This research builds upon prior work by its founders, as well as on the results obtained by Ashlagi, Immorlica, and Klein in 2009 and by Giannone, Gummadi, and Purohit in 2017. A previous study attributed this phenomenon to a recent galaxy-wide explosion, suggesting a constant density distribution for the gas in this galaxy. Using lattice QCD, a calculation of the two-flavor correlation function of the pion was performed to investigate its internal structure. This calculation yielded the distribution of two quark flavors within the pion, specifically for the distribution of up-down, up-up, and down-down pair correlations within the pion. These results demonstrate that the distribution of up-down pair correlations within the pion is nearly uniform, with a mean distance of approximately 0.4 fm, while the distributions of up-up and down-down pair correlations within the pion exhibit a peak at a much shorter distance of about 0.1 fm. This latter finding is consistent with earlier lattice QCD results indicating that the distribution of quark flavors within the proton exhibits a peak for same-flavor pair correlations at a similar distance. This calculation also permitted an examination of the dependence of these results on the mass of the quarks used in the lattice QCD simulation, with the findings indicating that the shape of the pion remains unaffected by changes in the mass of the quarks, whereas the size of the pion does change slightly in response to these changes. This conclusion holds for both light and strange quarks. Evaluating accretion rates in young stellar objects is crucial for understanding how disks influence rotation. However, measuring accretion rates is challenging due to variability of spectral lines. While many stars show stable or mildly variable spectral lines, we found unusual large fluctuations in the CT1 line of the XX Cha star. Analyzing CT1 line data from six instruments over the course of 14 years, we found a high dispersal of accretion rates, both when comparing results from different lines and combining our new data with previous measurements using the [Ca II] line. High dispersal in CT1 line data is unlikely to be caused by either instrument limitations or errors in measurements. Instead, it appears to result from significant variations in accretion flow over the observed time frame. If occurring in other stars, similar behavior could explain the high dispersal of accretion rates in some samples. Observing XX Cha over a shorter period of four years, we found a marked decrease in dispersal of accretion rates, suggesting that accretion variability may also depend on other factors such as stellar rotation period. A model incorporating both rotation period and duration of accretion bursts accurately predicts dispersal of accretion rates in XX Cha, but further research is needed to determine its broader applicability. If general, this model implies that dispersal of accretion rates in other stars could also be influenced by both variability time scales and duration of accretion bursts. The limited data set precludes drawing a definitive conclusion about its validity, but it does highlight the importance of monitoring both accretion variability time scales and duration of accretion bursts in other stars. If both time scales and duration of accretion bursts are monitored in other stars, future research could assess the role of both variables in determining dispersal of accretion rates in young stellar objects. The limited data set also prevents determining the exact time scales of variability and necessary duration of accretion bursts in XX Cha, but it does suggest that both may be shorter than typical values found in other stars. The unusual behavior of XX Cha may be linked to its low mass and the associated effects of both rapid rotation and a young stellar rotation period on its planetary system. Despite significant progress in reinforcement learning, learning from raw data offline remains a difficult task. Especially when considering multi-agent settings, where learning collaborative trajectories is crucial. This research addresses a key challenge: learning positive trajectories from isolated offline data without a matching counterfactual dataset. Our innovation includes two distinct contributions. Firstly, a method is developed to extract high-quality trajectories from large datasets, bypassing the need for a matching counterfactual set. This is achieved by constructing a balanced mixture of initial policy trajectories and exploratory natural baseline behavior. Secondly, a new algorithm called Balanced Trajectory Augmentation (BTA) is introduced. BTA utilizes this mixture to enhance the effectiveness of trajectory augmentation. Trajectory augmentation is a common practice where a initial policy is trained using a combination of reinforced experiences. However, this method can be ineffective when the initial policy has already converged to a suboptimal state. Our empirical evaluation of BTA on complex multi-agent offline datasets demonstrates its superiority over alternative methods. Code for BTA is available at https://github.com/GoogleResearchBrainTeam/BTA. This research also explores two critical applications of BTA: learning from limited positive data in zero-shot multi-agent settings and combining online and offline data in multi-agent settings. These experiments highlight the versatility and effectiveness of BTA. This work is part of the authors' ongoing research aimed at developing efficient methods for learning from positive trajectories in offline multi-agent settings. The notion of single-particle entanglement might seem benign, given that it involves the sharing of two particles prepared in an entangled state. However, research highlights that single-particle entanglement can give rise to genuine nonlocal effects, including the phenomenon of single-particle steering. This phenomenon, where the state of one particle is affected based on a measurement made on the other, distant particle, cannot be achieved through local operations. A recent study demonstrates single-particle steering in both spin and beam splitting scenarios, showing that even when the total number of particles is odd, it is possible to create single-particle steering through entanglement swapping. This achievement underlines the significance of single-particle entanglement and its associated nonlocal effects, also highlighting that even the most basic forms of single-particle entanglement hold considerable value for quantum information processing. This includes utilizing it for genuine nonlocal effects like single-particle steering, as well as for secure communication through the means of entanglement swapping. Consequently, single-particle entanglement should be highly prized in the creation of complex, multi-partite states and for implementing a variety of quantum information protocols. This achievement also highlights that the threshold for recognizing single-particle entanglement, often considered to be two particles, is too limiting and should be set lower, with a proposed threshold of one particle. This new perspective on single-particle entanglement offers a significant expansion on the original understanding of this concept, presented initially by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen in 1935. This new perspective also paves the way for exploring the sharing of single-particle entanglement among multiple, distant parties, as well as the creation of non-local connections among diverse, closed quantum systems. The increasing deployment of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has generated an enormous amount of transportation data, making it a precious asset for various intelligent transportation system applications. Nevertheless, IoV data is frequently distributed across multiple entities, complicating privacy preservation techniques. Although machine learning models can be highly effective for transportation data analysis, they require a considerable amount of data, posing a significant challenge in IoV settings. To address these difficulties, researchers and engineers have turned to federated learning, particularly in IoV contexts, where data remains localized across various vehicles and infrastructure. As privacy preservation becomes increasingly crucial, researchers have explored the integration of blockchain technology with federated learning to create secure and decentralized data management systems. Currently, various blockchain-based federated learning frameworks have been developed to support IoV applications, with notable examples including smart contract-supported FL and a combination of edge computing and blockchains. However, there are also challenges associated with these systems, including performance optimization, trustworthiness, and data privacy breaches. This review paper delves into the core challenges of IoV data analysis, the fundamentals of federated learning, and the integration of blockchain technology with FL. It also examines the existing literature on blockchain-supported FL in IoV settings, presenting a comprehensive overview of the various frameworks and protocols used. Furthermore, this review highlights the gaps in existing research, presenting opportunities for future investigations into this subject. This comprehensive survey of blockchain-supported FL in IoV contexts is anticipated to provide a valuable foundation for developers and researchers seeking to establish secure and private machine learning models using IoV data. This work also outlines a conceivable future research agenda for this domain. This review paper has been published in the journal Computers and Security, volume 122. In wireless communication systems, relay technology enhances coverage and increases data transfer rates. As a result, binary phase shift keying (BPSK) relay networks have been suggested as an alternative to orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems with high security risks. However, these systems are vulnerable to eavesdropping and need additional protection measures. This paper examines the security risks of BPSK relay networks and presents a new detection approach to increase the physical layer security. An eavesdropper's signal power estimate is first obtained by accumulating the powers of all subcarriers. Then, a normal approximation is used to create a confidence interval for this estimate based on the distribution of the sum of chi-squared variables. This allows for the identification of subcarriers that may be subject to eavesdropping. An alternative detection approach for these subcarriers is then proposed. This method involves determining the index of the subcarrier with the maximum side lobe in the time-frequency domain and marking the corresponding subcarriers as vulnerable to eavesdropping. Another approach involves examining the time-domain and frequency-domain side lobes of the signal and identifying the subcarriers with large side lobes as being subject to eavesdropping. This paper also presents simulation results showing the effectiveness of these detection approaches in BPSK relay networks. It is worth noting that BPSK relay networks are uncommon in practice and are generally replaced by more widely used modulation techniques like 16-QAM. However, this research is relevant to land mobile satellite communications, particularly in scenarios with rapid multipath fading and deep time-domain fading. Moreover, the proposed detection methods can be adapted for use in OFDM systems with high security risks. This may occur when there are localized errors in channel estimation, data transmission, or both. This could happen in scenarios with rapid multipath fading, deep time-domain fading, or both. This may also occur when the system has a large bandwidth and high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which leads to a high security risk in both time and frequency domains. This paper proposes a new detection approach for these situations. It involves examining the time and frequency side lobes of the signal and identifying the subcarriers with large side lobes as being subject to eavesdropping. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 100 actions per second, largely because of how they process language.
Our new TextWorldExpress platform shatters this barrier by using advanced techniques for rapid text understanding, incorporating modern neural networks for just the language component, and allowing actions to be taken at a rate of up to 1 million steps per second.
In addition to its high speed, TextWorldExpress boasts a more compact collection of games, with over 500 existing TextWorld games converted to its format.
We also present preliminary results demonstrating that agents trained on TextWorldExpress transfer effectively to traditional TextWorld games, even after stretching their training to 1 million steps. 
This platform is designed to be a starting point for further innovation, and we invite the community to build upon it. 
TextWorldExpress is available at https://textworldexpress.org/. 
A related paper titled "Efficient Text-Based Learning with TextWorldExpress" has been submitted to IJCAI 2023.

To mitigate this challenge, a co-design approach for energy-efficient LSTM networks is proposed, incorporating an efficient Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition framework. Furthermore, a novel, compact LSTM module called the Hierarchical LSTM (HiLSTM) was developed, with a specially designed activation function called the Hierarchical tanh (HiTanh) function. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated in a video identification application using the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets, outperforming traditional LSTMs and other tensor decomposition methods. The designed HiLSTM network was also optimized for hardware implementation on an FPGA, resulting in a significant reduction in energy consumption and memory requirements. The proposed co-design approach offers valuable insights for both hardware and software engineers on how to efficiently develop energy-saving deep learning networks. The HiLSTM source code and design files are available online at https://github.com/aliemamimi/HierachicalLSTM. Saturn's polar atmosphere exhibits unique seasonal variations driven by the planet's axial tilt. The formation of polar vortices in the northern hemisphere during its summer supports the overall vortex hypothesis. We provide a significant extension to the local uniformity theorem from its initial formulation, specifically for the case of algebras with a characteristic 2 field basis. Our research reveals that a wide range of affine varieties in these algebras can be precisely defined using a limited set of rational functions, despite the absence of a suitable version of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz in its standard form. Moreover, we demonstrate that these varieties' invariants are determinants that can be computed using a particular type of permanent-based sums, which are known to be computationally efficient in characteristics 2 and 0. However, they become impractical in characteristics greater than 2. As a broader context, our findings fit within the framework of a theoretical approach to varieties that were initially proposed by Denef and Lojasiewicz. Within this framework, our results specifically focus on the semi-parametric local characteristic free invariants of varieties. As a particular example, we detail a step-by-step process for determining the Wronskian's and the Jacobi matrix's properties, which can be further extended to the hypermatrices' case. As a result, we demonstrate that a particular class of polynomials, namely the quadratic extensions of the linear polynomials, can be found using the Jacobi matrix's property of being nilpotent. This specifically occurs in characteristics 2 and 0, whereas in characteristics greater than 2 it requires the additional condition of depth 2. As a consequence, we are able to demonstrate the efficiency of the Birkhoff and the Vandermonde matrices' property of being invertible, which in turn allows us to prove the divisibility of the determinant of the Wronskian by the square of the x-coordinates' greatest common divisor. This particular result can be further generalized to the hypermatrices' case, which in turn enables us to establish the determinants' property of being equal to the square of the x-coordinates' greatest common divisor. This specific result on the determinants' property can be further extended to the varieties defined by the polynomial systems with the coefficients' greatest common divisor equal to 1. For the category of graded collections, we identify a natural full subcategory of the category of monoids in the product category, which we call the polarization of graded collections. Then, we establish that the embedding of this subcategory into the original category induces a composition of natural transformations connecting the free monoid functor on graded collections to the free monoid functor on monoids, with the composition factors as the inclusion map does. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this composition can be viewed as the universal extension of the unit map of the free monoid functor by the inclusion map. Next, we generalize this result to the context of weighted collections. Moreover, we demonstrate that the polarized graded collections are equivalent to the monoids in the product category, whereas weighted collections are not. Finally, we show that the result on graded collections can be obtained as a special case of a more general outcome concerning the category of monoids with a specified operation, yielding the weighted collections as the polarized version. Additionally, we establish that the free monoid functor on weighted collections factors as the composition of the weighted collection functor and the free monoid functor on monoids, with the factor functors forming a dual pair. Lastly, we explore some concrete examples of polarized collections.

Thorne using the method of local functional equations, and provide a alternative derivation drawing on the relationship between measures and orbital integrals, combined with the Iwahori decomposition of adele groups. We also examine the specific case of GL_2 over a number field. Additionally, we discuss the measure associated with the conjugacy class of a given matrix, and provide some basic results on the subject. Lastly, we offer some concluding remarks about the relevance of these results to the study of global functoriality.

The effectiveness of x-ray retrieval technology for analyzing plasmas in nuclear stages can be significantly enhanced by utilizing x-ray diffusion spectroscopy, a new method that combines traditional retrieval techniques with optical emission spectroscopy. This combination enables the precise measurement of electron temperature and density throughout a target's structure, even in deeply opaque nuclear stages. A new x-ray diffusion emulator has been developed to quicken the computation of retrieval signals in multi-dimensional spaces, allowing for the direct extraction of temperature and density profiles from retrieval coefficients. This technique has been applied to a specific antihydrogen scenario, with results showing that it is possible to recover precise information about the target's structure, specifically the radius and density profiles, from retrieval coefficients. However, there are limitations, and further research is needed to fully explore the capabilities and constraints of this method. Despite these constraints, x-ray diffusion retrieval spectroscopy has been found to be a highly effective tool for gathering detailed information about the structure of nuclear stages, and it is anticipated that it will be particularly beneficial for experiments involving antihydrogen. Although larger stages pose a problem for this method, research has shown that it may also provide information about the distribution of particles within the stage, despite this challenge. A new hybrid-mixed finite element method has been developed to simulate single-phase Darcy flow within porous media that contain fractures. This approach incorporates the use of discrete fractures, represented by lines for 2D scenarios or hyperbolic lines for 3D cases, and combines these with the elements of a mixed finite element method for the bulk porous media. The key aspect of this technique is the designation of specific regions within the finite elements as part of the fractures, which allows for a more flexible representation of flow within the fractures without the need for the standard restriction of aligning fractures with the boundaries of the finite elements. This technique enables the direct application of the continuity condition across the interfaces between the fractures and the bulk media, which results in a more accurate representation of flow within the fractures. This is in contrast to the conventional approach of designating the interfaces between the fractures and the bulk media as part of the boundary conditions, which can lead to a less accurate depiction of flow within the fractures, especially in scenarios where the fractures exhibit narrow channels. This new hybrid-mixed finite element method has the advantage of simplifying the treatment of flow within the fractures, which allows for a more flexible geometry of the fractures, but it also introduces additional degrees of freedom associated with the normal component of the velocity within the finite elements, which necessitates a more comprehensive discretization scheme. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on mislabeled training data. When used as a proxy task, such a model can be used to inspect the underlying sentence representations and discourses, providing insights into its performance and limitations. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that such a model can effectively identify complex discourses and highlight issues with current sentence models, particularly in handling ambiguous and multi-discourse contexts. A subsequent exploration of incorporating discourse-aware sentence models into the prediction task demonstrates the potential benefits of this integration. The code and model are available at github.com/thomsmith/DiscSense.

A key property of cubic graphs is that they can be divided into edge-disjoint 1-factors, a concept that extends to the realm of edge-colored graphs as a property known as strong edge-colorability. Our research aimed to explore the relationship between edge-recognition and the absence of small odd components in a particular class of edge-colored cubic graphs, namely those with a specific tinting of bipartite components. However, we have discovered a counterexample to a previously proposed general property of this type, and it turns out that there are infinitely many examples within this class that are recognizable but cannot exhibit a specific edge-colored 1-factor known as an 'edge-tint'. Moreover, these examples enable us to identify a new concept of strong edge-colorability called strong 2-edge-colorability, and it turns out that this property is equivalent to the absence of a particular component known as a 'double star'. Finally, our findings also imply that another related property known as double-strength is also a more demanding condition than it initially seemed, requiring the absence of a different type of component known as a 'bigon'. Our research thus discovers and explores these two newly identified graph components, the double star and the bigon, and it does so within the specialized context of edge-colored cubic graphs. The property of strong 2-edge-colorability can be realized through a process known as edge-partitioning, and our results conclude with an examination of the relationship between this process and another process known as 2-factorization. The results we have obtained also hold value outside the confines of edge-colored cubic graphs, making them broadly significant. The evidence we have presented takes the form of a constructed example rather than an empirical discovery, and as such, it belongs to the category of theoretical evidence. The term 'edge-tinting' was coined by the paper's author, and it has the potential to be a useful concept within the broader field of graph theory. Convolutional neural networks are highly susceptible to security breaches when used in sensitive applications that involve image classification, but have limited access to labeled data. Introducing malicious backdoors during the training process is a common and challenging issue. Researchers have explored various methods to counter this problem, especially those that utilize faulty hardware, but a formal security proof for a popular transductive learning approach called Activation Clustering (ACT) remains elusive. In response, this paper provides the first formal security guarantee that a certain ACT variant can resist a specific type of attacks that feed fake images with natural noise, as well as those that use a 20 times smaller amount of malicious input corresponding to an embedded pattern. Moreover, this variant of ACT delivers a 83 times improvement in accuracy to tolerance ratio compared to the existing state-of-the-art benchmark, especially when the number of clusters is set to 1000. Furthermore, this paper demonstrates that a Qiu-based hardware fault tolerance using activation interval supervision as a special case, which provides a significant level of security against various breaches, including those caused by the presence of new classes, but requires a more expensive training process. 
This work appeared in ICML 2021.

This paper proposes a numerical solution to the inverse problem of finding a missing boundary data for the Maxwell's equations based on the complete boundary control method. A parabolic approximation of the original problem is developed to obtain a stable and unique reconstruction of the missing data, and ultimately the original problem is recovered. Computational results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed method even in the presence of noise. This approach provides a feasible solution to the highly unstable and ill-posed problem of recovering missing boundary data for the Maxwell's equations. In the age of expanding data, selecting relevant information for combination is a pressing issue. Traditional methods that combine all available data often result in subpar performance due to inclusion of noisy or misleading information. While recent studies have explored data selection techniques, they are largely developed assuming a supervised setting and lack consideration for federated scenarios. Our work addresses these shortcomings by introducing FEDSEL, a federated learning framework focused on selective data combination. Collaborating parties initially prepare a local subset of high-quality data, which is then used to train a shared model. FEDSEL incorporates an additional layer in the model to learn a weighting function for further refining the data combination process. Our proposed method is evaluated through Federated Learning and Adaptive Federated Learning experiments, and the results show promising performance improvements over baseline models. The code for FEDSEL is available at https://github.com/lingyu1995/FEDSEL.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz scattering microscopy to analyze planar microwave resonators used in quantum circuits. Terahertz nanoscopy, in particular, allows for the non-invasive examination of geometric information within the resonators, uncovering previously unappreciated sources of decoherence caused by spatial variations in frequency and envelope formation due to dielectric edges. We demonstrate that terahertz nanoscale resolution is necessary to detect and analyze local defects and edge effects and that this might pose a significant obstacle for scalable quantum computing. We also explore various resonator designs aimed at reducing the impact of decoherence. We recommend that future research include simultaneous investigation of frequency and envelope formation to comprehensively address decoherence in quantum systems. Lastly, this study highlights the value of terahertz nanoscale resolution for uncovering frequency information in nanophotonic devices used in quantum information. We further explore the relationship between dielectric edges and the formation of stop gaps in resonators and the effects of these edges on scattering, fermionization, and soliton formation in Bose-Jullien models. We show that in models with long-range interactions, the influence of edges on frequency and behavior can differ significantly. We propose experimental verification of our findings using terahertz scanning near-field optical microscopy. We also discuss possible extensions of this research to other systems, including photonic, mechanical, and cold atomic systems. We conclude by discussing the potential for future work, including the investigation of resonators with defects created by ion implantation, the study of edge-induced soliton formation, and the exploration of quantum systems with long-range interactions. We propose that future research in this area could lead to a deeper understanding of decoherence and could provide a framework for designing and analyzing quantum systems and uncovering frequency information in nanophotonic devices. We believe that this could be particularly relevant for silicon-based quantum systems, including quantum simulators and universal quantum computers. A key aspect of exoplanetary research is determining atmospheric development patterns in developing planetary systems. This study focuses on simulating the development of Venus's atmosphere using the LISO code and explores various scenarios for atmospheric development, including those driven by initial cloud cover, solar energy, and geological activity. Our findings reveal that the atmosphere on Venus has undergone a prolonged process of chemical and physical changes, and that different initial conditions can lead to similar present-day atmospheres with high surface temperatures and dense clouds. We also identify three key phases in the development of Venus's atmosphere: an initial rapid phase characterized by high levels of greenhouse gas release and atmospheric expansion; a secondary phase marked by increased cloud cover and a switch to oxidizing conditions; and a third phase, still uncertain in its details. This three-phase structure is stable under a range of conditions, although the specific processes and timescales can vary. This research highlights the complex interconnection between geological, chemical, and thermal processes in developing planetary systems and suggests that the atmosphere on Venus may be the result of a delicate balance between processes that release greenhouse gases and those that absorb them. This is particularly relevant for exoplanetary research, where there are many examples of super-Earth planets with atmospheres that may be subject to similar processes and feedback systems. This study provides a framework for understanding these processes and their interactions in these systems. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of independent Gaussian errors in a multiple-message scenario with additive white Gaussian noise. Our main finding shows that the error threshold of these codes exceeds the previously known record by an order of ten when the number of rows in the parity-contrast matrix is small and odd, say e.g. k=5, which significantly improves the codes' resistance to rank errors. Moreover, our research reveals that the optimal performance is achieved when the number of rows in the parity-contrast matrix coincides with the number of messages. Additionally, we demonstrate that the error threshold can be further enhanced by employing codes with multiple layers of row distributions, thereby greatly expanding the reliable communication distance beyond the previously established limit. Our results also imply that the optimal row distribution maximizes the error threshold at a certain point, which, however, does not result in the error threshold decreasing as the number of rows continues to increase, thereby providing a dynamic framework for evaluating and improving the performance of real-code implementations. Our study also highlights the relationship between the error threshold and the Kronecker coefficients, which may be of independent interest. The research also highlights the fundamental link between the error threshold and the Kronecker coefficients, which may be of value to the broader scientific community. We obtained comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo, an supernova that exploded in January 2020, in the nearby galaxy NGC 1431, which is approximately 96 million light years from Earth. Initially, we observed a rise in brightness over two weeks, followed by a short plateau phase of about 30 days, and then the typical decline seen in Type II SNe. The SN entered the nebula phase, shining brightly for an extended period of 130 days. SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent H-alpha line with a double-peaked profile in its early stages, and the expansion velocities of these peaks were distinct, with 13,000 km/s for the higher frequency peak and 6,000 km/s for the lower frequency peak. The electron temperature and abundance of elements like helium, heavy metals, and iron group elements in the SN's gas remained nearly constant. The abundance of elements like oxygen, carbon, and silicon varied significantly, with the highest velocities found for silicon, followed by oxygen and then carbon. The SN's gas expanded at an average velocity of 12,000 km/s and its optical depth was high enough to produce the Balmer lines of hydrogen through recombination, although it wasn't sufficient to absorb most of the ultraviolet light. The presence of the [Fe III] line suggests that the last generated electrons interact with a high degree of ionization, leaving behind mostly iron group elements. The formation of the [Fe III] line also indicates that the SN's gas has a complex structure, with different regions of varying density. To greatly decrease the number of photons required to detect a signal in X-ray monitoring tasks, a novel detector concept called the "lobster-eye lens array" has been proposed. This configuration utilizes a grid of pinhole cameras, also known as "lobster-eye lenses," to achieve wide-field coverage. Each lens in the array would be connected to a separate signal channel, significantly increasing the detector's sensitivity in low-flux environments. If each lens has its own amplifier, even in the presence of crosstalk, the system's sensitivity can be optimized for a specific signal source by adjusting the gain on each channel. This concept has been applied to a real detector, the eROSITA X-ray telescope, which will undergo launch in 2023 and will utilize this design to scan the sky for transient X-ray sources. Although primarily developed for this particular telescope, the lobster-eye lens array concept can be adapted for other transient X-ray monitoring applications, such as space-based and ground-based systems, following the eROSITA mission. The prelaunch performance of eROSITA, along with its expected postlaunch performance, will be reviewed. The challenges of background reduction faced by the detector will also be explored. The eROSITA team plans to make raw data publicly available one year after the mission concludes, which will enable researchers to recreate any detected signals and facilitate transient X-ray monitoring across the sky. The scalable design of the lobster-eye lens array detector also makes it suitable for other observational bands, such as optical and gamma-ray monitoring. The system's efficiency in detecting signals can be enhanced further by utilizing machine learning algorithms on the raw data, which would allow it to effectively discover transient sources across the sky for a much longer period than currently possible. The raw data from the eROSITA mission will be accessible through the Strasbourg Sky Catalogue Service. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving convergence in the solution for rotating stars under the theory of general relativity. We have successfully applied this method to model both rapidly and slowly rotating stars in both Newtonian and relativistic contexts. Our results for static stars, as well as rotating stars in both the slow and rapid rotation limits, match previously published research. The formation of massive stars is the most mysterious process in the universe, and the early stages of its development are critical to its overall comprehension.  While it is known that massive stars form from massive molecular cores, the specific path from core formation to star formation remains unclear.  One popular theory suggests that massive stars are born from dense clusters where cores and protostars collide and combine, leading to the formation of massive protostars.  However, there is limited direct observational evidence to support this theory.  Using a groundbreaking method that combines submillimeter interferometry with machine learning, researchers were able to uncover the historical development of a massive protostar called OMC-2 by dissecting a 0.1 parsec region surrounding a young star named $\theta$ Orionis.  They discovered a 0.01 parsec group of small, newly formed protostars that are in the same stage of development as OMC-2, and a massive protostar called ORI-K2 that is more developed.  Further analysis of this data revealed that OMC-2 formed about 30,000 to 40,000 years ago and went through a brief, intense accumulation period before which it had no associated matter.  This is the first direct observation of the initial stages of a massive protostar and reveals that its development was significantly more rapid than expected, taking only about 30,000 years.  Additionally, it showed that dense clusters can form massive protostars through the accumulation of multiple colliding cores, and that these protostars can then collapse into low-mass and high-mass star formation in different proportions, depending on factors such as density and gas removal mechanisms.  This finding provides a clear pathway for massive star formation and offers insights into the short timescales involved, as well as the critical role of dense clusters in forming both low-mass and high-mass stars.  It also raises questions about the likely outcomes of similar collisions in other regions, and suggests that massive protostars may be more common in regions with narrow beam widths than currently observed.  This study used a unique approach to investigate this case, but other methods such as spectroscopic analysis or multi-epoch surveys may provide similar insights in other regions.  Overall, it has significantly advanced our understanding of massive star formation and has identified key areas for future research in this field. Autonomous navigation, especially for challenging situations like in heavily flooded areas, poses a significant problem for robots to overcome. One key component of navigation systems is slam algorithms, which currently struggle to perform well in highly distorted environments. This research presents a novel method for using sonar sensors in flooded environments. Unlike conventional approaches, it bypasses the traditional mapping and inference process, instead feeding a motion control module with blended sonar readings that take into account the likelihood of false positive reflections from flooded areas. This method enhances navigation system performance and accelerates future development of capable autonomous underwater navigation solutions. Experimental results, conducted both indoors and outdoors, demonstrate the effectiveness and adaptability of this approach. A custom underwater robot, designed to operate in partially flooded environments, serves as a proof of concept for this navigation system. This navigation system has the potential to be adapted for other similar difficult terrain navigation tasks. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/utk-ailab/sonar-nav.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms, where misleading information can rapidly spread and cause real-world consequences. Since the content of counter measures often takes the form of text, recent advances in natural language processing, particularly in text generation, open up possibilities for our detection system to be more effective. In this research, we leverage text summarization to enhance fraudulent news detection by training a BERT-based model to distinguish between authentic and counterfeit news, and employing the summary of a post to feed the model, which yields a score used for classification. This research paper uses Gaussian random field theory to analyze the effects of bending waves on underwater sensors by an underwater vehicle. While the potential benefits of using surface-penetrating sensors are substantial, the challenge of detecting internal turbulence within moving targets under uncertain ocean conditions limits widespread adoption. To make these sensors more practical for daily use, we need a better understanding of how internal turbulence affects the vehicle's appearance from sensor data. Firstly, we established an equation to represent the relationship between the vehicle's internal and external properties using Gaussian random fields. Then, we investigated the impact of uncertainty in the vehicle's structure on the coherence of its scattered signals by analyzing the cross-spectral density between sensors. Our findings suggest that the vehicle's appearance remains stable across a wide range of ocean conditions if its internal configuration is relatively consistent. Consequently, we propose that sensors placed near the vehicle's surface, where bending waves are prominent, may be sufficient to infer its internal structure. Finally, we demonstrated that these sensors can detect the vehicle's shape and structure with high accuracy, provided they are placed within 10 times the wavelength of the longest wave present in the vehicle. To achieve this, we advise vehicles to carry sensors in pods embedded in their surfaces to cover a broad range of frequencies and speeds, up to 10 speeds per second. Traditionally, annotated datasets are considered static and cannot be modified.
However, annotated datasets can benefit from revised annotations, especially those
containing subjectively defined concepts like emotion-related labels.
We propose a novel approach, BERT-SAR, that leverages BERT to revise annotated
data, specifically emotion-related labels, and our evaluation reveals a positive
impact on the performance of subsequent tasks utilizing these revised labels.
Further analysis indicates that BERT-SAR excels in addressing labeling errors,
though it may introduce unwanted variation when dealing with ambiguous or context-dependent
emotional expressions.
Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/BERT-SAR.

This research explores a fundamental aspect of mixture models where probability distributions are combined, specifically those from a finite set of components whose identities are unknown. A key challenge in this context is identifying the number of mixture components and their corresponding distributions. To address this issue, a method based on geometric analysis was developed, which determines the number of components by examining the shape of a curve derived from the mixture model and verifies the accuracy of this approach through simulated data and real-world examples. The proposed method can be difficult to implement due to its reliance on advanced numerical techniques, but it provides a theoretical foundation for this problem that can be used to extend and refine the method. A notable application of this method is in image processing, specifically deblurring texts, but it has the potential to be adapted across various fields beyond image processing. Recent advancements in deep learning have been significantly boosted by using NVIDIA GPUs for object-oriented programming.  Despite this progress, memory management on GPUs remains a major obstacle for large-scale deep learning models, particularly those utilizing object-oriented frameworks.  Current GPU memory managers, designed to automate memory allocation, also limit the parallelism that can be achieved by wasting current GPU capabilities, such as multi-object arrays.  In response to these challenges, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator that leverages the full potential of NVIDIA GPUs, including their capability to manage large scales of deep learning models using object-oriented development.  Our allocator employs a novel, lock-free page division scheme that reduces memory waste and increases parallelism, as well as a unique, asynchronous memory reclamation strategy that boosts performance in long-lived allocations.  We apply DynaSOAr to real-world object-oriented deep learning frameworks and baselines, achieving a 24% performance boost in TensorFlow and a 15% performance boost in PyTorch.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr outperforms the current state-of-the-art GPU memory allocator, TAO, by 12% in TensorFlow and 8% in PyTorch.  Our results demonstrate that DynaSOAr is a high-performance, efficient memory allocator that effectively utilizes the capabilities of NVIDIA GPUs for object-oriented development.  Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/IBM/DynaSOAr.  We also present optimization guidelines for converting popular object-oriented deep learning frameworks to use NVIDIA GPUs.  Our analysis reveals that DynaSOAr achieves a 25% performance improvement in TensorFlow by converting multi-object arrays to base data types.  Our results demonstrate the significant performance gains that can be achieved by utilizing NVIDIA GPUs for object-oriented development, as well as the challenges and opportunities for future research in this area.  We propose the term "object-oriented GPU development" (OOGD) and present the OOGD benchmark suite, consisting of popular object-oriented deep learning frameworks, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, as well as new, object-oriented GPU-based algorithms for natural language processing and computer vision tasks.  Our analysis of the OOGD benchmark suite on various NVIDIA GPUs reveals that current object-oriented deep learning frameworks fail to achieve high levels of parallelism, as well as memory management issues that limit their performance.  We believe that the OOGD benchmark suite will aid in the development of more efficient memory allocators and object-oriented deep learning frameworks that utilize the full potential of NVIDIA GPUs. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This initial principles method, applied to a single magnetic impurity, yields the spectral functions for all relevant states including the Kondo effect, the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) state, and the little--Maxwell--Goppert--Yahr state. When considering two magnetic impurities, the model predicts YSR, two-Goppert--Yahr, and two-Maxwell--Yahr states, depending on the spacing between the impurities and their alignment. This theoretical framework enables the interpretation of experimental data from the YSR states induced by manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface. The results show that a single manganese adatom supports a localized YSR state at the Fermi level, while a pair of adatoms placed far apart will each support a YSR state at the Fermi level, but with their spins coupled in a ferromagnetic arrangement when aligned side by side. In contrast, two adatoms located close to one another will have their YSR states shifted away from the Fermi level and will also exhibit Rabi oscillations between the YSR and Goppert--Yahr states. This theoretical analysis is compared to recent experimental results, where the YSR states induced by manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface were studied using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The experimental data agree with the theoretical predictions, displaying YSR, Goppert--Yahr, and Maxwell--Yahr states for single, side-by-side paired, and closely paired adatoms, respectively. The interaction between the YSR states of the paired adatoms can vary depending on their alignment, which enables the distinction between two key situations:  a situation where the YSR states are associated with a single YSR state with a large amplitude when the adatoms are aligned side by side, and a situation where the YSR states are associated with two separate YSR states with smaller amplitudes when the adatoms are close to each other. The exchange interaction between the adatoms can be either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic in nature, which represents a new development in the study of magnetic dimers. The distinction between these two situations can be determined by rotating the magnetization vector, which will cause the YSR states associated with the side-by-side paired adatoms to exhibit either four-fold or two-fold rotation symmetry, respectively. By applying this metric to simulate a massless Dirac cone using qutrits, we find that it is challenging to achieve satisfactory results, however, we do observe the emergence of "sound" in simulations using four-level systems. An alternative strategy called the "truncation expansion" is explored to investigate the behavior of the massless Dirac cone in the low-energy regime. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the specific case of polarized positrons has yet to be explored in detail. Our study examines the polarization characteristics of positrons emitted when a highly intense laser beam interacts with a particular type of target, namely a carbon foil preceded by a thin layer of gold. We find that, when the number of generated positrons becomes very high, the polarization of the positron stream reaches its maximum possible value, specifically 3.86%, independent of the initial conditions. This happens when the number of positrons produced exceeds 10^8 per square millimeter. Notably, the polarization of the positrons shows minimal dependence on the specifics of the target material used. This indicates that, in the limit of very high positron densities, the polarization pattern becomes a reliable inherent property of the positrons themselves, rather than being influenced by the complex dynamics of the electron-positron pair generation process. This crucial insight paves the way for optimizing positron polarization in a wide range of scenarios, exceeding the confined context examined here. This is particularly significant because, as we demonstrate, it's possible to create extremely dense positron clouds at high densities, far surpassing any previously reported results. This achievement is all the more notable given that, as we show, the necessary conditions for achieving the highest polarization levels are actually less stringent than those required to produce the same levels of positron density without polarization. This offers a promising breakthrough for a wide range of applications and uses of dense polarized positrons. This work is accompanied by an executable code that allows for further exploration and modification of the results presented here. This code is based on the most recent version of the ELDKAW complex particle simulator developed by A. MacCowan. This version was specifically optimized for high-performance computing. A group's algebraic diameter is defined as the minimum number required to express the group's identity element as a product of group elements. This research introduces the concept of a group of finite diameter, exploring its implications. It is demonstrated that a finite group with a diameter of one is a cyclic group, implying its structure is based on a single generator. A similar conclusion holds for groups with a diameter of two, demonstrating they are either abelian groups with at least three generators or the alternating group A5, depending on whether they possess triple relations or not. Additionally, this work provides an invariant that upper-bounds a group's diameter and offers finite groups with a finite diameter in relation to specific properties. Moreover, it is proven that the geometric dimension three, denoted as GDT3, property is connected to finite groups with a finite diameter, ending at the alternating group A5. This leads to the conjecture that the algebraic diameter of the alternating group A5 is indeed finite. This research expands the framework of finite groups with a finite diameter, presenting open problems and potential lines of inquiry. It is notable that the term 'finite diameter' was previously used, with the term 'of finite diameter' being the proposed expansion. As integrated temperature detection becomes more prevalent in CMOS technology, the likelihood of temperature-related errors in signal processing increases.  A novel approach is proposed to incorporate a small temperature detection circuit into the source follower input stage of an analog-to-digital converter.  This circuit utilizes a mismatched PMOS resistor in the feedback loop to create a temperature-dependent voltage, which results in a temperature reading available at the ADC input.  Experimental validation of the proposed design shows a 3.5x improvement in temperature sensitivity, with a measured temperature range of 0.6V to 1.8V, a 0.24 degrees C resolution, a 1.4 degrees C error margin, and a conversion energy of 1.06 nJ.  This research was published in the IEEE International Solid-State Circuits Technology Conference (ISSCC) in 2023.

The flow behavior of liquid foams is significantly influenced by the texture of their surface.  A recent study revealed the existence of a particular cell wall regime, characterized by a sudden and marked increase in friction.  This phenomenon was found to result from the unique interaction between the vertical cell walls and the moving surface, creating an asymmetrical pattern as the surface flows to the sides.  This pattern consists of channels and sinuses, and its stability is critical in understanding the abrupt increase in friction.  A computational analysis showed that the emergence of this pattern can be attributed to the sudden appearance of a sticky state in the cell wall texture.  This sticky state is induced by the sudden increase in the radius of curvature of the cell walls and results in a sharp and significant escalation in frictional forces.  The resulting cell wall texture also exhibits a complex dynamics, with channels and sinuses continuously merging and splitting.  This complex behavior is stable and has been observed in repeated experiments, demonstrating the robustness of this texture-induced regime.  It also gives rise to a distinctive sound emission, likely a hallmark of this regime.  A computational analysis of the cell wall texture allows for the extraction of relevant information, enabling the prediction of the onset of the sticky state, the cell size distribution, and the sound emission phenomenon.  This knowledge provides a deeper understanding of the intricate dynamics of liquid foams and offers a novel approach to controllably varying their texture-induced behavior.  The possibility of transferring this knowledge to other complex systems with similar cell-like structures is also discussed.  The possible connections to other phenomena, such as granular gases, dry friction, and nonlinear oscillations, are explored in the companion paper by van Hoogman et al. titled: Nonlinear Dynamics of a Liquid Foam Surface.  The study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters vol. 125, no. 12 (2020).
